title: Procedural Law Case: Shivnath Shah Kanu v. Vishwanath Shah Kanu, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Procedural Law Case: Shivanath Shah Kanu vs. Vishwanath Shah Kanu, NKP 2069 B.S., D.N. 8820   Case: Case related to property and appellate procedure Plaintiff/ Applicant: Shivnath Shah Kanu Defendant/ Respondent: Vishwanath Shah Kanu Decision Number. 8820  

This case is related to the partition of the ancestral property and the classification of acquired property alongside the statutory right of appeal and the legal effect of multiple appellate decisions arising from the same judgment.

  Facts of the Case: The plaintiff, Vishwanath Sah Kanu, and the defendant, Shivnath Sah Kanu, were brothers whose parents had passed away. They were the only sons of Suraj Sah Kanu, who, along with their mother, had died before the institution of the suit. Before their father's death, Suraj Sah Kanu and his brother, Harihar Sah Kanu, the uncle, had already partitioned their ancestral property through a registered partition and had been living separately afterwards. The plaintiff claimed that, as a coparcener of the ancestral property, he demanded a fair partition of the property, believing that the defendant was attempting to conceal and withhold it. The plaintiff requested the court to determine the date of separation as the day preceding the filing of the suit, direct both parties to submit an inventory (तायदाती फाँटवारी) of all joint family properties, recognize that there were only two coparceners, allot one half share to him, and order registration of the allotted share in his own name. Here, the defendant accepted the relation but refused the partition of all the claimed property as some of the disputed properties were self-acquired, gifts of his own, and bought in the name of his sons, Rajesh and Manoj Prasad. As a result, the plaintiff filed a suit for partition in the court.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the disputed properties claimed by the defendant were self-acquired properties exempt from partition or ancestral properties liable to partition?
  2. Whether two conflicting decisions at the same appellate level can exist, and which one should be treated as valid?
  3. Whether procedural errors deprived the defendant of his right to appeal?
  Different Courts' Decisions: District Court: Bara District Court stated that there's no dispute regarding the relationship between the parties of the case or their status as coparceners. Hence, the plaintiff is legally entitled to a one half share of the property, so the property must be equally partitioned, and the plaintiff must be provided with the one half share of the partition. Appellate Court: Firstly, in the presence of a single party, the appellate court affirmed the decision in favor of the plaintiff. But later when defendant appealed to Appellate Court as the time limitation for appeal wasn’t expired, once again concerning the same issue, the court after reviewing the claim of the defendant in presence of both the party fulfilling the due-process, partly reversed the decision of the district court and separated few disputed properties to be self-acquired and gifts of the defendant pointing out the errors in plot numbers, making it not partitionable. Supreme Court: The Supreme Court stated that the court must ensure all parties have been granted their statutory right to appeal before concluding any case. It further stated that the earlier appellate judgment could not curtail the defendant's legal right to appeal, and if there is more than one decision passed from the same level due to a procedural irregularity, then the later judgment rendered following due process should be considered as the authoritative decision. Lastly, since the lower courts had not conclusively determined whether the disputed properties were self-acquired or ancestral, the Supreme Court directed that the matter be placed before a Joint Bench for final adjudication on those issues. Principle Established:
  • Only ancestral property is subject to partition, self‑acquired or gifted property cannot be divided unless proven otherwise.
  • An appellate court must ensure that every party's statutory right to appeal has been exhausted before finally disposing a case.
  • A judgment delivered on one party's appeal before the expiry of the other party's appeal period cannot curtail or nullify that party's statutory right of appeal.
  • Where two judgments are delivered in the same dispute because of a procedural error, the later judgment rendered after following due process and hearing both parties constitutes the authoritative decision.
Hence, this case is a significant case of Nepal in context of appellate procedures and partition of the property that establishes that in partition of property self-acquired, gifted property are required to be excluded and that in case of more than one judgement from the same level, the later one rendered in alignment with the procedural requirements must be adhered to.
rationale: Classification resolved to CASE_LAW, but subject cannot be determined safely.

title: Procedural Law Case: Tripuradevi Jha v. Kathmandu District Court, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Procedural Law Case: Tripuradevi Jha v. Kathmandu District Court, NKP 2057 B.S., DN: 6996   Case: Robbery-related case Plaintiff/Applicant: Tripuradevi Jha Defendant/Respondent: Kathmandu District Court Decision Number: 6996  

This case is concerned with robbery, where the Supreme Court examined the sufficiency of evidence to establish the punishable act.

  Facts of the Case: On 2049/09/09 at 10:30 AM, in the absence of the plaintiff's husband, the defendants entered the courtyard of the plaintiff and physically and verbally assaulted the plaintiff and her daughter. When they became unconscious, the defendants looted the plaintiff's house goods worth Rs. 1,405, including:
  • 480 worth of rice (Manasuli variety)
  • 425 worth of wheat
  • 200 worth of two steel plates
  • 200 worth of two brass pots (lota)
  • 100 worth of one bucket (walteen)
The plaintiff filed the case seeking compensation for the looted goods and punishment of the defendants. The defendants denied the allegations of robbery, stating that they are purely the outcome of personal enmity. Upon analyzing the evidence and witness testimonies, including a separate assault (Kutpit) case (Criminal. Reg. No. 661) arising from the same incident had already been decided by the Janakpur Appellate Court on 2052/3/1, holding the defendants guilty of assaulting the plaintiff, and that decision had become final. This prior judgment served as corroborative evidence in the looting case. So, District Court had ruled in favor of the plaintiff, finding the defendants guilty of robbery, the Janakpur Appellate Court reversed this decision and acquitted the defendants. The plaintiff then appealed to the Supreme Court. Here, due to the dissatisfaction of the plaintiff with the decisions delivered, the case was appealed to the Supreme Court.   Legal Issues:
  1. Did the prosecution prove the offence of robbery beyond the required standard of proof?
  2. Was the Appellate Court mistaken in dismissing the looting charge despite corroborating evidence?
  3. Are proceedings conducted under the ordinary procedure instead of the Summary Procedure Act, 2028, invalid?
  Different Courts’ Decisions: District Court: District Court found the defendants guilty of looting and ordered the defendants to pay compensation and imposed the prescribed punishment. This decision was based on the categorical testimony of the plaintiff's witnesses, Birendra Mitra and Maharudra Jha, who had clearly stated the date, time, and details of the stolen goods, thereby corroborating the plaintiff's claim. Appellate Court: The Appellate Court reversed the decision of the District Court, stating insufficiency of evidence to establish the crime. Supreme Court: The Supreme Court allowed the plaintiff's appeal and set aside the Appellate Court's judgment. It held that Section 14 of the Summary Procedure Act, 2028, provides that proceedings are not invalid merely because the ordinary procedure was followed instead of the summary procedure. The court reinstated the decision of the district court, stating that the plaintiff has provided sufficient evidence alongside the corroborated evidence from a related case of assault, finding the five defendants guilty of robbery and charging them with the prescribed punishment and compensation for stolen property.   Principle Established:
  1. Proceedings are not merely invalid due to procedural technicalities (summary vs. general procedure), as this does not invalidate substantive justice.
  2. A conviction for robbery can be based on credible and consistent eyewitness testimony when supported by corroborating evidence.
  3. A final judgment in a related criminal case may be relied upon as corroborative evidence to establish the occurrence of the incident.
  4. Mere denial by the accused, without supporting evidence, is insufficient to rebut credible prosecution evidence.
This case is significant because it clarifies that procedural irregularities do not automatically invalidate criminal proceedings where the law expressly provides otherwise. It also reinforces that consistent eyewitness testimony corroborated by independent evidence, including findings from a related criminal case, is sufficient to establish the offence of robbery.
rationale: Classification resolved to CASE_LAW, but subject cannot be determined safely.

title: Juvenile Delinquency Case: Advocate Aashish Adhikari on behalf of Bablu Godia v. Banke District Court et al, (5th Semester)
content:
Juvenile Delinquency Case: Advocate Aashish Adhikari on behalf of Bablu Godia v. Banke District Court et al, Writ no. 3390 of the year 2057 BS, Date of Decision: 2057/12/12 BS.   Case: Writ of habeas corpus Plaintiff: Advocate Aashish Adhikari on behalf of Bablu Godia Respondent: Banke District Court et al Writ no: 3390 of the year 2057  

This case is related to detention of juvenile in adult prison.

  Facts of the case: A charge sheet was filed against the petitioner Mr. Bablu Godia (aged 14 at the time of offence) and other persons for committing an offence referred in No. 6 of the country code chapter on theft.  The Banke District court & Nepalgunj Appellate Court found him guilty & was placed in the adult prison facility and kept indiscriminately together with adult offenders. Following a prior Supreme Court verdict directing his transfer to a Child Reform Home, he was removed from the adult jail but was instead placed into an even more difficult detention cell because a proper Reform Home was not functioning. As a result, a fresh writ petition of Habeas Corpus was filed in the Supreme Court on his behalf. The writ petition was filed pursuant to Articles 23 and 88(2) of the constitution of the Kingdom of Nepal, 2047 (1990).   Legal issues:
  1. Whether detaining a juvenile (a child under 16 years of age) indiscriminately in a regular prison alongside adult offenders violates the protections guaranteed under domestic child rights legislation and international conventions?
  2. Whether the state is legally obligated to immediately establish and place children in conflict with the law into specialized Child Reform Homes rather than adult prisons or substandard detention cells?
  Decision of the courts: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court ruled against the respondents, explicitly condemning the practice of keeping the child in an adult jail facility with adult criminals. The Supreme Court issued an order to the Government to immediately transfer the juvenile detainee to a Child Reform Home. The Court ruled that if a proper reform facility does not exist, the Government must make necessary arrangements to establish one immediately.   Principles Established:
  1. Children in conflict with the law cannot be treated as adult offenders or mixed with adult prison populations. They must be kept in separate, child-appropriate environments to avoid negative psychological impacts and criminal contamination.
  2. The government cannot use the absence of specialized institutional facilities (like reform homes) as an excuse to hold minors in adult jail facilities or regular detention cells. The state has an absolute legal duty to create and maintain the necessary infrastructure required to enforce the Act Relating to Children.
  Relevance of the Case: This landmark case domesticated international juvenile justice standards in Nepal, permanently prohibited mixing children with adult inmates and forced the state to build functioning Child Correction Homes (Bal Sudhar Griha).   Source: Baseline Survey on Juvenile Justice System In Nepal, 2010 {KSL JOURNAL}

title: Juvenile Delinquency Case: Advocate Aashish Adhikari on behalf of Keshav Khadka v. HMG et al (5th Semester)
content:
Juvenile Delinquency Case: Advocate Aashish Adhikari on behalf of Keshav Khadka v. His Majesty's Government, Ministry of Home Affairs et al, Writ no 70 of the year 2058 BS, Date of Decision: 2058/12/13 BS   Case: Writ of habeas corpus and mandamus Plaintiff: Advocate Aashish Adhikari on behalf of Keshav Khadka Respondent: HMG et al Writ no: 70 of the year 2058  

This case is related to juvenile reform home.

  Facts of the Case: The petitioner, Keshav Khadka, was a minor (14 years old) who had previously been ordered by the Supreme Court of Nepal to be kept at the Juvenile Reform Home (Bal Sudhar Griha) in Sanothimi, Bhaktapur rather than a regular adult prison cell. While residing at the reform home, he was enrolled in a nearby school in the 8th Grade and preparing for his annual examinations. In total disregard of the Supreme Court’s prior ruling and his ongoing education, authorities later extracted him from the reform home and placed him back with adults in the jail. The authorities justified this through bureaucratic oversights, claiming a lack of space, administrative convenience. After which, the writ petition was filed by Adv. Aashish Adhikari (working under the Free Legal Aid project of CeLRRd) challenging the legality of removing a minor from a rehabilitation center and placing them back with adults.   Legal issues:
  1. Whether the state can legally house or transfer a minor child into an adult prison facility after a court has mandated placement in a child reform center?
  2. Whether interrupting a juvenile's education and rehabilitation by placing them in an adult prison violates their fundamental rights under the Children Act, 2048 (1992) and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC)?
  Decision of the courts:  Supreme Court: The Supreme Court reinforced its stance on juvenile protection, ruling against the detention of the minor in an adult prison facility. The court ordered the relevant authorities to ensure the petitioner remained or was returned to a juvenile appropriate environment (the child reform home) to ensure his physical protection, mental well-being, and the continuation of his schooling and upcoming examinations.   Principles Established: This case established the principle that all administrative and judicial actions concerning minors must prioritize their rehabilitation, education, and welfare over punitive incarceration.   Relevance of the Case: This case serves as a key piece of evidence demonstrating that even when the Supreme Court issues orders, justice sector actors and prison administrations frequently relapse into traditional punitive behaviors (e.g., shifting children back to adult facilities due to administrative convenience or lack of institutional capacity). Source: Baseline Survey on Juvenile Justice System in Nepal, 2010 {KSL JOURNAL}

title: Juvenile Delinquency Case: Pleader Tara Devi Khanal on behalf of Raj Kumar Rai vs. Ministry of Home Affairs et al (5th Semester)
content:
Juvenile Delinquency Case: Pleader Tara Devi Khanal on behalf of Raj Kumar Rai v. Ministry of Home Affairs et al, Writ no 25 of the year 2058, Date of Decision: 2058/10/02 BS   Case: Habeas Corpus writ petition regarding  juvenile justice Plaintiff: Pleader Tara Devi Khanal on behalf of Raj Kumar Rai Respondent: Ministry of Home Affairs et al Writ Number: 25 of the year 2058  

This case is related to juvenile reform homes.

  Facts of the Case: Raj Kumar Rai was a 12 year old child originally from Namobuddha Village Development Committee, Kavrepalanchowk, living in a rented house in Kathmandu. A charge sheet was filed against him before the Kathmandu District Court on July 30, 2001. On Shrawan 16 2058, the Kathmandu District Court issued a detention order under Number 118 of the Chapter on Court Management, ordering him to be sent to adult prison custody because he could not provide a required cash deposit/bail. A writ of habeas corpus was filed on his behalf by Pleader Tara Devi Khanal (representing the Free Legal Aid Programme for Prisoners conducted by CeLRRd), arguing that detaining a 12 year old child in an adult jail violated the explicit provisions of the Children's Act, 2048 (1991).   Legal issues:
  1. Whether a child under the age of 16 can be lawfully detained in an adult prison or jail facility under standard adult criminal procedures (such as Number 118 of the Chapter on Court Management) for failing to deposit bail?
  2. Whether the court and prison authorities violated Section 15 and Section 42 of the Children's Act, 2048 (1991), which guarantee alternative treatment, separate confinement, and placement in juvenile reform homes for minors?
  Decision of the Courts: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court upheld the writ petition. The Court observed that under Section 11(3) of the Children's Act, a child of Raj Kumar's age is only liable for a maximum of half the punishment awardable to an adult. By the time of the hearing, the child had already spent a highly disproportionate time in detention under adult jail conditions. The Supreme Court ordered his immediate release from adult prison custody and mandated that any necessary institutional care or custody be arranged in a designated child reform home or under authorized guardianship, strictly following the Children's Act.   Principles Established:
  1. Children under the age of 16 cannot be housed alongside adult inmates in standard jails, regardless of their financial inability to post bail.
  2. The specific protective provisions of the Children’s Act, 2048 override general procedural provisions when dealing with minors.
  3. The state must strictly bound judicial custody and sentences to the maximum statutory provisions provided for children.
  Relevance of Case: This case is a landmark precedent in Nepalese juvenile jurisprudence highlighting the insensitivity of the justice system at the bail hearing stage. It emphasizes that children in conflict with the law must be provided a reformative and rehabilitative environment rather than exposure to criminals in adult prisons which directly increases the vulnerability to recidivism. Source: Baseline Survey on Juvenile Justice System In Nepal, 2010 {KSL JOURNAL}

title: Juvenile Delinquency Case: Adv. Santosh Kumar Mahato vs. Office of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers et al., NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Juvenile Delinquency Case: Adv. Santosh Kumar Mahato vs. Office of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers et. al, Writ No. 60 of the year 2061 BS, Date of Decision: 2062/10/09 BS, NKP 2064, DN: 7578   Case: Mandamus writ petition regarding juvenile justice Plaintiff: Adv. Santosh Kumar Mahato Respondent: Office of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers et. al Decision Number: 7578  

This case is related to the formation of specialized Juvenile Courts and the proper composition of Juvenile Bench.

  Facts of the Case: The Act Relating to Children 2048 and its Rules, 2051 were enacted to safeguard the rights and holistic development of children. Section 55 of the Act outlines the framework for a dedicated Juvenile Court, providing that until such a court is formed, each District Court must establish a Juvenile Bench comprising a District Judge along with social workers, child experts or child psychologists. On 2056/12/28, the Ministry of Women, Children and Social Welfare published a notice in the Nepal Gazette designating a Juvenile Bench in all districts consisting solely of the District Judge effective from 2057/01/01. The petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 88 of the Constitution of the Kingdom of Nepal, 2047 arguing that a bench consisting only of a judge violates Article 11(3) of the Constitution, Section 55(5) of the Act and Articles 12 and 40 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), 1989. The petitioner also claimed that the state had failed to fulfill its statutory duty and a prior court commitment from a 2054 writ petition to establish an independent Juvenile Court.   Legal issues:
  1. Whether the government's gazette notice of 2056/12/28 regarding the formation of the Juvenile Bench contradicts the Constitution of the Kingdom of Nepal, 2047, the Act Relating to Children, 2048 and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, 1989?
  2. Whether a mandamus or directive order should be issued to establish dedicated Juvenile Courts and effectively monitor the order's execution?
  Decision of the Court: Supreme Court: As stated in Section 55(1) of the Act Relating to Children 2048, the responsibility to establish a juvenile court lies within the government. Accordingly, a directive order is issued in the name of the Office of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers to speed up the establishment of a juvenile court in accordance with that legal provision and to inform the Decision Implementation Branch under the Monitoring and Inspection Division of this Court of its action. A directive order was issued to the Decision Implementation Branch to actively oversee the execution of this directive. Hence, the writ petition was upheld.   Principles Established:
  1. The juvenile bench which was established until the juvenile court was formed is not a permanent structure. It cannot be assumed that the government has fulfilled its duty by establishing only the juvenile bench without addressing the main structure, i.e. the juvenile court.
  2. Given that the Act itself has prioritized the establishment of a juvenile court and a written commitment to establish one has been made 5 years ago, the short-term arrangement regarding the establishment of a juvenile bench cannot be considered to have fulfilled the obligation of the government.
  Relevance of the Case: The case reinforces the mandatory nature of establishing distinct juvenile justice institutions over stopgap administrative measures. It marks a critical step toward implementing specialized juvenile courts in Nepal rather than relying solely on default district courts.

title: Juvenile Delinquency Case: Mahesh Kumar Chaudhary v. Government of Nepal, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Juvenile Delinquency Case: Mahesh Kumar Chaudhary v. Government of Nepal, NKP 2064, P. 145, DN: 7833   Case: Incest Rape Plaintiff: Government of Nepal on the complaint of Minaki Kumari Khaa Chaudhary Respondent: Mahesh Kumar Chaudhary Decision Number: 7833  

This case is related to incest rape & juvenile delinquency.

  Facts of the Case: On 2055/01/24, the applicant, Minaki Kumari Khaa Chaudhari was raped by Mahendra, who was her elder brother (cousin) within three generation. Based on school records and a medical evaluation report, the defendant was between 12 to 14 years old at the time of the commission of offense. She was lured to go to the field on the pretext of the seeds on the field being eaten by goats. He raped her in the field after she was made unconscious after the beatings. The victim was slapped on cheek, towel stuffed in her mouth & threatened to not shout, or else she would be killed. Ishwarwati Tharuni (villager) saw the incident taking place & she spread the information in Shalikram Chaudhari’s shop which was near the scene of incident. The offender fled after he saw Tharuni. The victim was rescued by the help of villagers. The medical examination which was conducted after 7 days of the incident stated “congestion and redness over vulva vaginal post and slightly oozing”.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the general provisions of the Muluki Ain (No. 10 of the Chapter on Rape) or the specific provisions of the Section 11(2) of Act Relating to Children, 2048 apply to a minor defendant who has committed an offense?
  2. Whether the confiscation and transfer of half of the defendant's property (Ansha Sarbaswa) to the victim constitutes an economic penalty and whether such a financial liability can legally be imposed on a minor under 14 years of age?
  Decision of the Court: District Court: Sunsari District Court sentenced him to 6 months in prison under the Act Relating to Children, 2048. In accordance with No. 11(a)(2) of “Danda Sajaya’, if the defendant agrees to pay Rs. 45,000 at the rate of Rs. 750 per month, then the sentence is to be decreased. Since the defendant was under 14, his property cannot be confiscated. Appellate Court: The Appellate Court altered this & included the mandatory confiscation of half of his property to award it as compensation to the victim. Supreme Court: Supreme Court denied the prosecution's demand to award half of the defendant's ancestral property to the victim stating that further punishments under general law do not apply to minors under 14. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction and the 6-month prison sentence but quashed the order to confiscate and transfer half of the minor defendant's property to the victim as it was a violation of Section 11(2) of the Act Relating to Children, 2048.   Principles Established:
  1. The two roles of the state are noteworthy in controlling crime. First, to effectively administer the law to control crime and second, to punish the person who is found to be breaking the law.
  2. The Act Relating to Children, 2048 was enacted as a law to adopt a reformative punishment system because it is inappropriate to punish children who act without knowing the consequences of their actions as severely as adults.
  3. Since the defendant was 12-14 years old at the time of the crime, the law itself exempts him from being punished financially, and they cannot be punished financially on the pretext of giving compensation contrary to the law by using a model of financial punishment like a fine. Paying compensation is also a type of financial punishment. Generally, compensation does not have a prominent place in the criminal justice system.
  4. The judgment of giving half of the defendant's property to the victim as a compensation according to No.10 of the Chapter on Rape is contrary to the intention of the legal provision in Section 11(2) of the Act Relating to Children, 2048.
  Relevance of Case: The case involves a minor defendant aged 12–14 convicted of incest. It established that property forfeiture is an economic penalty from which minors are legally exempt.

title: Family Law Case: Rabindra Kami v. Tilottama Kami, NKP (4th Semester)
content:
Family Law Case: Rabindra Kami v. Tilottama Kami, NKP 2062 B.S., Vol.4, D.No. 7528   Case: Cancellation of deed, establishment of ownership and registration (Likhit Badar, Hak Kayam and Da. Kha. registration) Plaintiff: Rabindra Kami Defendant: Tilottama Kami et al. Decision Number: 7528  

This case is related to the validity of a sale deed executed by a mother over ancestral property and whether such transfer violates the rights of other coparceners.

  Facts of the Case: The plaintiff, Rabindra Kami, was the son of Tilottama Kami. The disputed property originally belonged to his father and, after his father's death, was registered in his mother's name. Ravindra claimed that he and his mother were the only coparceners of the ancestral property. While Rabindra was working in India, his mother sold a piece of the ancestral property (Kitta No. 65, measuring 0–5–1–1 along with the house built on it) to Bir Bahadur Kami without informing or obtaining his consent. Ravindra believed that the sale was intended to deprive him of his inheritance rights and therefore filed a suit seeking cancellation of the sale deed and recognition of his share in the property. The defendant, Tilottama Kami, denied the allegation and argued that she sold the property to meet household expenses, repay family debts, and support the family's livelihood because Ravindra was living in India and was not contributing to the family. She further claimed that the law allowed a person managing the joint family to sell property within the legal limit without the consent of the other coparceners. Since the lower courts did not fully accept Ravindra's claim, he ultimately appealed the matter before the Supreme Court.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether a mother managing household affairs can sell ancestral property without the consent of her son/co-sharer.
  2. Whether the sale was within the legal limit allowed under Section 19(1) of the Partition Law.
  3. Whether the Appellate Court was correct in partially cancelling the deed (one-fourth cancellation).
  Decision of the Courts:                                                                       District Court (Tanahun): The District Court held that the defendant, Tilmata Kami, being the head of the household, had sold the property for necessity and that the plaintiff’s claim was not valid. It dismissed the case. Appellate Court (Pokhara): The Appellate Court held that although the mother could manage household affairs, she could only dispose of property within legal limits. It therefore partially allowed the claim and ordered cancellation of one-fourth of the deed while upholding the remaining portion. Supreme Court of Nepal (Division Bench): The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Appellate Court. It held that the mother was responsible for household management as the plaintiff was abroad and no other co-sharers were practically involved in management. The Court found that under Section 19(1) of the Partition Law, a person managing household affairs can dispose of up to half of ancestral immovable property without consent of other co-sharers. Since the property sold was within this legal limit, the Court held that there was no legal ground to fully invalidate the deed. It also held that the Appellate Court correctly applied the law by partially cancelling only a portion of the deed. Therefore, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the Appellate Court.   Principle Established: A household manager may dispose of up to half of ancestral immovable property for household necessity without the consent of other co-sharers under Section 19(1) of the Partition Law. If the disposal remains within this statutory limit, the sale deed cannot be cancelled, and courts must consider both legal authority and necessity before invalidating the transaction.   Relevancy of the Case: This case is important because it explains how much power a person managing a joint family has to sell ancestral property. The Supreme Court held that such a person can sell only the portion allowed by law and cannot take away the inheritance rights of the other family members. It protects the rights of co-sharers while allowing property to be sold for genuine family needs.
rationale: Ambiguous Family Law record. No explicit evidence distinguishing Family Law-I vs Family Law-II.

title: Family Law Case: Puspa Raj v. Nepal Government, NKP (4th Semester)
content:
Family Law Case: Puspa Raj v. Nepal Government, N.K.P. 2074 B.S., Vol.59, D.N: 9757   Case: Writ Petition (Certiorari and Mandamus). Petitioner: Puspa Raj Pandey Respondents: Government of Nepal, Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers & Others Decision Number: 9757  

 This Case relating to Commercial Surrogacy, Women's Rights, Reproductive Technology, and Regulation of Assisted Reproductive Technology.

  Facts of the Case: In 2071/06/02 B.S., the Government of Nepal (Council of Ministers) decided to allow Nepali hospitals to provide surrogacy services to foreign citizens, even though Nepal did not have any law regulating surrogacy. After this decision, some hospitals, including Grande City Clinic and Hospital, started offering surrogacy services. Concerned about this, Advocate Puspa Raj Pandey filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) before the Supreme Court. He argued that the Government could not introduce surrogacy simply through a Cabinet decision without first passing a law through Parliament. He also claimed that commercial surrogacy could exploit poor women by treating motherhood as a business. Therefore, he asked the Supreme Court to cancel the Government's decision, stop hospitals from providing surrogacy services, and direct the Government to enact a proper law regulating surrogacy. In response, the Government stated that the National Health Policy, 2071 only proposed that surrogacy would be regulated by a future law and did not itself authorize hospitals to provide such services. It also argued that no hospital had been officially licensed because the necessary legal procedures had not yet been prepared. While the case was pending, the Supreme Court issued an interim order stopping the implementation of the Government's decision. Later, on 2072/06/01, the Government cancelled its earlier decision. Even so, the Supreme Court continued to hear the case because it involved important issues of public interest and stressed that Nepal should enact a comprehensive law to regulate surrogacy.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the Government could legally authorize surrogacy through a Cabinet decision without a law enacted by Parliament.
  2. Whether commercial surrogacy is consistent with public policy, morality, and the protection of women's rights.
  3. Whether Nepal requires a comprehensive law to regulate surrogacy services.
  Decision of the Court: Supreme Court of Nepal: The Supreme Court held that the Government could not introduce surrogacy through a Cabinet decision without a law passed by Parliament. It observed that commercial surrogacy could exploit women and raise serious legal, ethical, and public health concerns. Although the Government had already cancelled its earlier decision, making the writ petition unnecessary, the Court directed the Government to enact a comprehensive law allowing only altruistic surrogacy under strict legal safeguards and prohibiting commercial surrogacy.   Principle Established: This case established that surrogacy can be allowed only through a law passed by Parliament, not by a Cabinet decision. It also established that commercial surrogacy should not be permitted because it can exploit women and is against public policy and morality. If surrogacy is allowed in Nepal, it must be regulated by a clear law that protects the rights of the surrogate mother, the child, and the intended parents.   Relevancy of the Case: This case is important because it is Nepal's leading Family Law case on surrogacy. It clarified that commercial surrogacy cannot be allowed without a proper law and highlighted the need to protect women from exploitation and children from legal uncertainty. It also guided the Government to enact a comprehensive law for regulating surrogacy in Nepal.
rationale: Ambiguous Family Law record. No explicit evidence distinguishing Family Law-I vs Family Law-II.

title: Family Law Case: Narayan Prasad Tharu v. Harendra Kumar Chaudhary, NKP (4th Semester)
content:
Family Law Case: Narayan Prasad Tharu v. Harendra Kumar Chaudhary, NKP 2076 B.S., Vol. 61, DN: 10394   Case: Establishment of Inheritance Right (Aputali Hak Kayam) Plaintiff: Indra Kumari Devi Chaudhary (through her authorized representative, Harendra Kumar Chaudhary) Defendant: Narayan Prasad Tharu Decision Number: 10394  

This case is related to the inheritance rights over a deceased woman's property, where the Supreme Court decided whether a married biological daughter or a stepson has the stronger legal claim to inherit her estate.

    Facts of the Case: Shankar Tharu had two wives. His first wife, Soniya Devi, had a son, Narayan Prasad Tharu, while his second wife, Saguni Devi, had one daughter, Indra Kumari. After Shankar's death, his property was jointly registered in the names of Saguni Devi and Narayan Prasad. When Saguni Devi later died, Narayan Prasad transferred her share solely into his own name, claiming that as her stepson and a member of the joint family, he alone was entitled to inherit it. Indra Kumari, Saguni Devi's only biological daughter, claimed that her mother's share should pass to her under the law of inheritance. The dispute ultimately reached the Supreme Court. Legal Issues:
  1. Whether a married biological daughter or a stepson is the closer legal heir to inherit the property of a deceased woman.
  2. Whether the absence of partition between co-sharers prevents inheritance rights from arising.
  3. Whether joint ownership of property automatically transfers the deceased co-owner's share to the surviving co-owner.
  4. Whether marriage disqualifies a biological daughter from inheriting her mother's property.
  Decision of the Courts: Nawalparasi District Court: The District Court dismissed the plaintiff's claim. It held that since Saguni Devi and Narayan Prasad had never partitioned their property and remained members of the same joint family, the married daughter could not claim inheritance over Saguni Devi's share. Butwal Appellate Court: The Appellate Court affirmed the District Court's judgment. It agreed that the married daughter had no inheritance right because the deceased's share had not been separated before her death. Supreme Court (Joint Bench): The Joint Bench reversed the decisions of both lower courts. It held that Saguni Devi's half share in the jointly owned property formed part of her estate and, after her death, passed to her only biological daughter, Indra Kumari, under the law of inheritance. Supreme Court (Full Bench): The Full Bench upheld the Joint Bench's decision. It ruled that a married biological daughter is the nearest legal heir to her mother's property and has priority over a stepson. The Court further held that inheritance and partition are separate legal concepts, joint ownership does not extinguish an individual's share, and marriage does not take away a daughter's inheritance rights.   Principle Established: A married biological daughter remains the nearest legal heir to her mother's property and cannot be excluded from inheritance merely because she is married. The Court clarified that inheritance rights are independent of partition rights, and a surviving joint owner cannot automatically acquire the deceased co-owner's share simply because the property remained jointly owned.   Relevancy of the Case: This case is an important precedent in Nepalese inheritance law. It clarifies that a married biological daughter has a superior inheritance right over a stepson in respect of her deceased mother's property. It also distinguishes inheritance from partition rights and reinforces the constitutional principle that a daughter's inheritance rights cannot be denied merely because she is married.
rationale: Ambiguous Family Law record. No explicit evidence distinguishing Family Law-I vs Family Law-II.

title: Family Law Case: Sukum Thapa v. Pitamber Thapa, NKP (4th Semester)
content:
Family Law Case: Sukum Thapa v. Pitamber Thapa, NKP 2076 B.S., Vol.61, D.No.10346   Case: Writ of Certiorari and Mandamus Petitioners: Sukum Thapa et al. Respondents: Pitambar Thapa et al. Decision Number: 10346  

This case is related to equal inheritance rights of married daughters, partition of ancestral property, the effect of a will (Shesh Pachhiko Bakaspatra) over undivided joint family property, and gender equality under the Constitution of Nepal.

  Facts of the Case: The dispute arose within the Thapa family over the partition of their ancestral property. Pitambar Thapa was the son of Nandamaya Thapa. He had several wives, including Chitrakumari Thapa (his first wife), Sukum Thapa (his second wife), and Raksha Thapa (his later wife). Manisha Thapa and Nisha Thapa were Pitambar Thapa's daughters. In 2052 B.S., Chitrakumari Thapa and Sukum Thapa filed a partition case after they were forced to leave the family home. On 2065/01/25, the Supreme Court decided that they and their daughters, Manisha and Nisha, were legally entitled to receive a share in the ancestral property. When the family property was later being divided according to that judgment, a new dispute arose. Pitambar Thapa claimed that his mother, Nandamaya Thapa, had given her share of the property only to him through a Shesh Pachhiko Bakaspatra (will) dated 2068/06/26. Later, Raksha Thapa produced another, much earlier will dated 2053/05/31, claiming that the same property had actually been gifted to her by the same woman, who was referred to as Rankumari Thapa. However Rankumari and Nandamaya was not same person, they both are separate person. Raksha Thapa has produced the will with illicit/bad intention. At the same time, Pitambar Thapa argued that his daughters, Manisha Thapa and Nisha Thapa, should not receive any share because they had already married in 2070 B.S. As the family disagreed over who was entitled to Nandamaya's share of the property and whether married daughters could still inherit ancestral property, the petitioners challenged the matter before the Supreme Court through the present writ petition.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether property received through a Shesh Pachhiko Bakaspatra before partition is subject to partition among all coparceners.
  2. Whether married daughters can be denied their share in ancestral property on the basis of marriage.
  3. Whether the High Court's order recognizing Raksha Thapa's claim under the earlier will was legally valid.
  4. Whether the High Court's order violated the constitutional right to equality and equal inheritance.
  Decision of the Courts:                                                                        Rupandehi District Court: The District Court refused to recognize the will allegedly executed by Runkumari (claimed to be Nandamaya) in favour of Raksha Thapa and held that Nandamaya's share should not be transferred exclusively to Raksha. It directed that the property be partitioned according to the Supreme Court's earlier partition judgment. High Court Tulsipur, Butwal Bench: The High Court reversed the District Court's order. It held that the earlier registered will in favour of Raksha Thapa was valid and excluded the married daughters, Manisha Thapa and Nisha Thapa, from the list of coparceners, directing the partition to proceed accordingly. Supreme Court: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order. It held that property received by a coparcener through a will while the family remained joint must be shared among all coparceners, and that married daughters cannot be excluded from inheritance merely because of their marriage. Accordingly, it ordered that Nandamaya's share be included in the joint family property and partitioned equally among all coparceners.   Principle Established: Property received by a coparcener through a will while the family remains joint continues to be part of the joint family property and must be shared among all coparceners. The case also established that married daughters cannot be excluded from ancestral property merely because of their marital status, as they enjoy equal inheritance rights under the Constitution and the law. Relevancy of the Case: This case is a landmark precedent in Nepalese family and inheritance law. It clarifies that property received through a will by a coparcener while the family remains joint must be shared among all coparceners and that married daughters cannot be denied inheritance solely because of their marital status. It also reinforces the constitutional guarantee of equal inheritance rights and prohibits gender-based discrimination in ancestral property.
rationale: Ambiguous Family Law record. No explicit evidence distinguishing Family Law-I vs Family Law-II.

title: Contract Law Case: Chitra Bahadur Karki v. Maniram Agrawal, NKP, (4th Semester).
content:
Contract Law Case: Chitra Bahadur Karki v. Maniram Agrawal, NKP, 2071, Vol. 10, DN. 9264.   Case: Meaning of Contract/ No Consideration No Contract. Plaintiff: Shubhakamana Construction & Concern, represented by Pro. Chitra Bahadur Karki. Defendant: Maniram Agrawal, Proprietor of Agrawal Industries. Decision Number: 9264  

This Case is related to Recovery of money under an alleged contract, Meaning of Contract, Consideration of contract.

  Facts of the Case: Shubhakamana Construction & Concern, operated by Chitra Bahadur Karki, had a government ration supply contract for Shree Shamsher Dal Gan Dah Barrack, Dadeldhura for the fiscal year 2059/060 BS. During the contract period, Chitra Bahadur Karki claimed that he suffered financial losses. When a new tender was invited for the fiscal year 2060/061 BS, both Chitra Bahadur Karki and Maniram Agrawal participated. According to Chitra Bahadur Karki, both parties signed a written agreement on 2060/08/01 BS, under which Maniram Agrawal would obtain the new ration contract and, in return, it would compensate Chitra Bahadur Karki by paying Rs. 13,00,000/- for ration purchase losses and Rs. 8,84,721.67/- for losses from meat, vegetable, and potato subcontracts, making a total of Rs. 21,84,721.67/-, payable within 30 days. Chitra Bahadur Karki alleged that Maniram Agrawal failed to make the agreed payment despite the agreement and therefore Shubhakamana Construction & Concern filed a suit to recover the amount. Maniram Agrawal denied the claim, stating that no valid contract had been made. He argued that he had only signed a blank page of Chitra Bahadur Karki's diary for another purpose and that Chitra Bahadur Karki later inserted false terms to create the disputed agreement. He further contended that the document did not satisfy the legal requirements of a valid contract and that Chitra Bahadur Karki had no legal authority to transfer or guarantee the government ration supply contract.   Plaintiff's Claim: Plaintiff claimed that, A valid written agreement dated 2060/08/01 BS. had been voluntarily executed between the parties. Maniram Agrawal had agreed to pay: Rs. 13,00,000/- towards ration purchase losses; and Rs. 8,84,721.67/- towards losses arising from meat, vegetable and potato subcontracts. Although payment was to be made within 30 days, Maniram Agrawal failed to fulfil his promise. Therefore, court should order Maniram Agrawal to pay the entire agreed amount. Defendant's Arguments: Maniram Agrawal argued that, no valid contract had ever been concluded with Chitra Bahadur Karki. He never agreed to compensate plaintiff. His signature had been obtained on a blank diary page for another purpose. Chitra Bahadur Karki later inserted false terms and fabricated the alleged agreement. The document did not satisfy the legal requirements of a contract. Chitra Bahadur Karki had no legal authority to transfer or guarantee the government ration contract to him.   Legal Issues:
  1. What essential elements must exist for an agreement to become a valid contract?
  2. Whether the agreement dated 2060/08/01 BS, between Chitra Bahadur Karki and Maniram Agrawal constituted a legally enforceable contract?
  3. Whether the judgment of Appellate Court was legally correct?
  Decisions of the Courts: Kailali District Court: It held that the agreement was genuine and ordered Maniram Agrawal to pay Rs. 13,00,000/- to Chitra Bahadur Karki it also imposed a fine of Rs. 100/- on Maniram Agrawal for alleging that the document was forged. Also rejected the claim relating to the additional losses from meat, vegetable and potato subcontracts. Dipayal Appellate Court: Reversed the judgment of Kailali District Court. It held that the agreement dated 2060/08/01 BS, was not a legally enforceable contract. Therefore, it dismissed plaintiff's claim.  Supreme Court: Supreme Court upheld the decision of Appellate Court and held that, the agreement between Chitra Bahadur Karki and Maniram Agrawal was vague and uncertain. It lacked lawful consideration. Chitra Bahadur Karki had no legal authority to promise or transfer the government ration contract. The agreement was impossible to perform legally. Therefore, it did not satisfy the essential requirements of a valid contract under the Contract Act, 2056. And Shubhakamana Construction & Concern was not entitled to recover any amount from Maniram Agrawal.   Established Principles:
  1. Not every agreement is a contract: Only an agreement fulfilling all legal requirements becomes enforceable.
  2. A valid contract must contain: competent parties, offer and acceptance, intention to create legal relations, lawful consideration, certainty and clarity, free consent, lawful object, possibility of performance, legal formalities.
  3. Unclear or vague agreements cannot become valid contracts.
  4. The principle "No Consideration, No Contract" applies in Nepal. A contract without lawful consideration is not enforceable.
rationale: Classification resolved to CASE_LAW, but subject cannot be determined safely.

title: Family Law Case: Dr. Rajaram Karki v. Usha Karki, NKP (4th Semester)
content:
Family Law Case: Dr. Rajaram Karki v. Usha Karki, NKP 2070 B.S., Vol.55, D.N: 9014 Case: Maintenance (Manachamal) Plaintiff: Usha Karki Defendant: Dr. Rajaram Karki Decision Number: 9014  

This case is related to maintenance (Manachamal). It clarifies that a husband has a legal duty to maintain his wife according to his financial capacity and explains how courts should determine a reasonable amount of maintenance.

  Facts of the Case: Dr. Rajaram Karki and Usha Karki were husband and wife. They had two sons and one daughter, and the daughter was already married. In 2063 BS, Rajaram allegedly forced Usha to leave the matrimonial home. Since then, she had been living separately and surviving with financial help from her parents and friends because she had no independent source of income. At the same time, Usha had already filed a separate partition (Ansha) case to claim her share of the family property, but that case had not yet been decided. Until she received her share, she requested the Court to order her husband to provide monthly maintenance (Manachamal) for her daily living expenses. Usha stated that Rajaram was a doctor who owned and operated his own diagnostic clinic and earned about Rs. 1,50,000 per month. Therefore, she claimed Rs. 18,000 per month as maintenance for herself and also asked for money to cover the educational expenses of their two sons studying abroad. Rajaram denied earning the amount claimed by Usha. He argued that he had taken large bank loans to run his clinic and was already facing heavy financial liabilities. He also stated that since Usha had already filed a partition case, she would eventually receive her share of the property, so he should not be required to pay the amount she demanded.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether a husband is legally bound to provide maintenance (Manachamal) to his wife according to his financial capacity.
  2. How should the Court determine a reasonable amount of maintenance?
  3. Whether the wife could also claim the educational expenses of their adult sons in a maintenance case.
  Decision of the Courts: Kathmandu District Court: District Court held that Usha had no independent source of income and was living separately after being driven out of the house. Since Rajaram was a doctor with sufficient earning capacity, the Court ordered him to pay Rs. 30,000 per month as maintenance. However, it rejected the remaining claim for a higher amount. Patan Appellate Court: The Appellate Court held that the wife was entitled to maintenance but found that the District Court had awarded more than what she had actually claimed. It also ruled that the educational expenses of the adult sons could not be awarded in this case because they had not filed any claim themselves. Accordingly, it reduced the maintenance amount to Rs. 18,000 per month. Supreme Court: The Supreme Court upheld the Appellate Court's decision. It held that a husband has a legal duty to maintain his wife according to his financial capacity. The Court observed that there is no fixed mathematical formula for determining maintenance; rather, it must be decided by considering the husband's financial condition and the circumstances of the wife. Since Rajaram had failed to prove sufficient grounds to reduce the amount further, the order directing him to pay Rs. 18,000 per month as maintenance was affirmed.   Principle Established: A husband has a legal duty to maintain his wife according to his financial capacity. The amount of maintenance is not fixed by any mathematical formula but is determined by the Court after considering the husband's income, financial condition, and the wife's needs. A court should also decide only the claims made before it and cannot award relief beyond the scope of the plaintiff's claim.   Relevancy of the Case: This case is an important precedent in Nepalese family law because it explains that maintenance (Manachamal) is a legal responsibility of the husband, even when a partition case is pending. It also establishes that maintenance should be fixed according to the husband's actual financial capacity and that courts must award only the relief specifically claimed by the parties while maintaining fairness between both sides.
rationale: Ambiguous Family Law record. No explicit evidence distinguishing Family Law-I vs Family Law-II.

title: Family Law Case: Sunil Babu Pant v. GON and Others, NKP (4th Semester)
content:
Family Law Case: Sunil Babu Pant v. GON and Others, NKP 2065 B.S., Vol. 50, D.N: 7958   Case: Public Interest Litigation (Writ Petition) Petitioner: Sunil Babu Pant (Executive Director, Blue Diamond Society) Respondents: Government of Nepal and Others Decision Number: 7958  

This is a landmark Public Interest Litigation filed by Sunil Babu Pant on behalf of LGBT and third gender persons seeking legal recognition of gender identity, protection from discrimination, and equal constitutional and human rights.

  Facts of the Case: The petitioner, Sunil Babu Pant, Executive Director of the Blue Diamond Society, filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) before the Supreme Court on behalf of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and third gender (LGBTT) persons. He argued that these individuals were facing discrimination, violence, social exclusion and unfair treatment because of their sexual orientation and gender identity. Since the law did not recognize third gender persons, they faced difficulties in obtaining citizenship certificates, passports and other official documents reflecting their self-identified gender. They also faced obstacles in accessing education, employment and other government services. Therefore, the petitioner requested the Supreme Court to recognize the rights of LGBTT persons, prohibit discrimination against them, direct the Government to amend discriminatory laws, and ensure equal protection of their constitutional and human rights. The petitioner also requested the Court to consider legal recognition of same sex marriage.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity violates the right to equality.
  2. Whether third gender persons have the right to legal recognition based on their self-identified gender.
  3. Whether the State must amend discriminatory laws affecting LGBTT persons.
  4. Whether Nepal's international human rights obligations protect LGBTT persons from discrimination.
  5. Whether the Government should study and consider legal recognition of same-sex marriage.
  Decision of the Courts: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court held that discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity is unconstitutional and violates the fundamental rights to equality, dignity, freedom, and non-discrimination. The Court recognized the legal identity of third gender persons and directed the Government to issue citizenship and other official documents reflecting their gender identity. It also ordered the Government to review and amend discriminatory laws, form a committee to study laws relating to same-sex marriage, and enact appropriate legislation to protect the rights of sexual and gender minorities.   Principle Established: The case established that every person is entitled to equal rights, dignity, and legal protection regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. The State cannot discriminate against individuals simply because they belong to a sexual or gender minority, and it has a constitutional duty to recognize and protect their rights through appropriate laws.   Relevancy of the Case: This case is one of Nepal's most important human rights decisions. It recognized the constitutional rights of LGBTI and third gender persons, strengthened the principle of equality and non-discrimination, and laid the foundation for future legal reforms relating to gender identity, citizenship, and family rights. It is frequently cited in constitutional, family law, and human rights jurisprudence.
rationale: Ambiguous Family Law record. No explicit evidence distinguishing Family Law-I vs Family Law-II.

title: Family Law Case: Sudhansu Koirala vs. Snidha Mainali, NKP (4th Semester)
content:
Family Law Case: Sudhansu Koirala vs. Snidha Mainali, NKP 2077 B.S., Vol. 62, D.N: 10482   Case: Domestic Violence Appellant/Defendant: Sudhansu Koirala Respondent/Plaintiff: Snidha Mainali Decision Number: 10482  

This case is related to domestic violence within marriage, including physical, mental, and sexual abuse, the doctrine of continuing offence, and the victim's right to treatment expenses and compensation under the Domestic Violence (Crime and Punishment) Act, 2066.

  Facts of the Case: Dr. Snidha Mainali and Dr. Sudhansu Koirala, both medical doctors, were married on 2069/08/14 in accordance with social customs and traditions. Shortly after their marriage, disputes arose between them. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant had concealed his sexual incapacity before the marriage and, thereafter, whenever this issue was raised, he became angry and started physically assaulting, threatening, and mentally harassing her.She further alleged that one of the assaults resulted in a fracture of her tailbone and that the defendant also created disturbances at her workplace and clinic, causing her humiliation and emotional distress. Claiming that she had been subjected to continuous physical, mental, and sexual abuse amounting to domestic violence under the Domestic Violence (Crime and Punishment) Act, 2066, she filed a complaint against her husband and also implicated her father-in-law and mother-in-law for their alleged involvement. She sought punishment of the defendants, along with treatment expenses and compensation as provided under the Act.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the defendant committed domestic violence under the Domestic Violence (Crime and Punishment) Act, 2066.
  2. Whether the plaintiff's complaint was filed within the statutory limitation period.
  3. Whether the plaintiff was entitled to both treatment expenses and compensation under the Act.
  Decision of the Courts: Kathmandu  District Court: District Court held that Dr. Sudhansu Koirala had committed domestic violence to his wife, Dr. Snidha Mainali by physically assaulting and mentally abusing her after marriage. The Court held that such acts amounted to domestic violence under Section 3 of the Domestic Violence (Crime and Punishment) Act, 2066, which defines physical, mental, emotional, sexual, and economic abuse committed by one family member against another. Accordingly, the Court convicted Dr. Sudhansu under Section 13, which provides punishment for committing domestic violence. It also ordered him to pay all medical treatment expenses under Section 9 and provide compensation under Section 10 for the physical and mental suffering caused to his wife. However, the allegations against his father and mother were not proved, so they were acquitted. Patan Appellate Court: Appellate Court upheld the District Court's judgment, affirming the defendant's conviction, punishment, treatment expenses, and compensation. Supreme Court: Supreme Court dismissed the defendant's appeal and affirmed the lower courts' judgments. It held that domestic violence includes physical, mental, sexual, and emotional abuse, recognized continuous domestic violence as a continuing offence, and ruled that treatment expenses and compensation are distinct remedies that may be awarded simultaneously. It also emphasized a gender-sensitive, human rights-based interpretation of domestic violence laws.   Principle Established: Supreme Court held that domestic violence is not limited to physical assault but also includes mental, emotional and sexual abuse within marriage. It recognized continuous domestic violence as a continuing offence and emphasized that marriage must be based on equality, dignity, and informed consent, and held that treatment expenses and compensation are separate remedies that may be awarded simultaneously.   Relevancy of the Case: This is a landmark decision on the interpretation of the Domestic Violence (Crime and Punishment) Act, 2066. It broadened the scope of domestic violence by recognizing physical, mental, sexual, and emotional abuse within marriage, treated continuous domestic violence as a continuing offence for limitation purposes, affirmed that treatment expenses and compensation are independent remedies, and emphasized a gender-sensitive, human rights-based approach to the protection of victims.
rationale: Ambiguous Family Law record. No explicit evidence distinguishing Family Law-I vs Family Law-II.

title: Juvenile Delinquency Case: Advocate Kalyan K.C. on behalf of Saroj Rai vs. District Administration Office, Kathmandu et al. (5th Semester)
content:
Juvenile Delinquency Case: Advocate Kalyan K.C. on behalf of Saroj Rai vs. District Administration Office, Kathmandu et al., Writ no. 0025 of the year 2066 BS, Date of Decision: 2066/06/26   Case: Habeas Corpus  Petitioner: Advocate Kalyan K.C., working at the International Legal Foundation on behalf of Saroj Rai  Respondents: District Administration Office, Kathmandu; Chief District Officer (CDO) and Prison Office, Jagannath Dewal, Kathmandu Writ No: 0025 of the Year 2066 BS  

This case is related to the jurisdiction over minor offenses and the unlawful detention of juveniles in adult prisons.

  Facts of the Case: The petitioner, Saroj Rai was a 14 year old minor. He was arrested by Metropolitan Police Circle under Section 2(a) of the Act Relating to Children, 2048 on 2066/06/10. He was kept in police custody until 2066/06/16 and subsequently produced before the District Administration Office for a Public Offense (Public Peace) charge. On 2066/06/20, the CDO ordered a bail amount of Rs. 5,000. Because the minor was unable to pay, the CDO ordered him to be sent to the Juvenile Reform Home in Bhaktapur for pre-trial detention. However, due to lack of space, the reform home turned him away. Consequently, on 2066/06/21, he was sent to the Central Jail (Jagannath Dewal) and detained alongside adult prisoners. The petitioner filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that the CDO lacks jurisdiction under Section 55(2) of the Act Relating to Children, 2048 to try cases where a minor is the sole defendant. The petitioner claimed that the detention ordered by an executive authority violated constitutional provisions on personal liberty, child rights, the Act Relating to Children, 2048, and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), 1989. The respondents argued that the Some Public Offense (Punishment and Control) Act, 2027 explicitly empowers the CDO to hear public offense cases to maintain social peace and that the minor was sent to the regular prison only after the juvenile reform home lacked physical space.   Legal Issues: 
  1. Whether the Chief District Officer (CDO) has the legal authority and jurisdiction to hear and adjudicate a Public Offense case where the sole defendant is a minor under 16 years of age?
  2. Whether the writ should be issued to release Saroj Rai from detention?
  3. Whether specific orders or directives need to be issued regarding pending cases of a similar nature?
  Decision of the Court:  Decision of Supreme Court: Supreme Court held that under Section 55(2) of the Act Relating to Children, 2048, and Article 40(2) of the UNCRC, offenses involving minors as sole defendants must be tried strictly by a Juvenile Court or a Juvenile Bench within a District Court. Therefore, the Supreme Court quashed the CDO's bail order of Rs. 5,000 and transferred the ongoing case directly to the Kathmandu District Court for a lawful trial. Regarding the plea for immediate release under habeas corpus, the Court declined to release the minor outright because criminal charges were active. Since the case was being transferred to a competent judicial body (the District Court) which would re-evaluate the evidence, facts and detention necessity under child friendly laws, an outright release via extraordinary jurisdiction was deemed inappropriate. To that extent, the habeas corpus request was quashed. Additionally, the Court issued a directive to the Ministry of Home Affairs to immediately identify and transfer all pending juvenile-only cases from CDOs across all districts to their respective District Court Juvenile Benches.   Principles Established: 
  1. It is not possible for civil servants to try criminal cases in a state that is a party to conventions like the ICCPR and the CRC and has a written constitution that provides for fundamental rights.
  2. According to the constitutional system, the law that was valid until yesterday cannot remain valid even after the constitutional system has changed.
  3. Since the provision that the Chief District Officer also tries cases where the only defendant is a minor under the age of 16, the right of the Chief District Officer to try cases where the only defendant is a minor under the age of 16, as per Section 5 of the Public (Crime and Control) Act, 2027, will be invalid 
  4. The power given by Section 5 of the Some Public (Crime and Control) Act, 2027 to the CDO is limited up to adults only. It can’t hear the case involving an only minor defendant as it is contrary to Article 40(2) (ii) (iii) of the CRC and Section 55 of the Children's Act, 2048 and such act will be invalid from the date of the decision by Prospective Overruling.
  Relevance of Case: This landmark case restricts executive overreach by stripping Chief District Officers of their quasi-judicial powers to try and detain minors under the Public Offense Act. It establishes the doctrine of prospective overruling regarding historical executive-led trials of children.   Source: Baseline Survey on Juvenile Justice System In Nepal, 2010 {KSL JOURNAL}
rationale: Title clearly represents distinct academic subject (Juvenile Delinquency) absent from Prisma.

title: Juvenile Delinquency Case: Advocate Sapana Pradhan Malla on behalf of Forum for Women, Law and Development (FWLD) and on her own behalf vs. Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers et al, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Juvenile Delinquency Case: Advocate Sapana Pradhan Malla on behalf of Forum for Women, Law and Development (FWLD) and on her own behalf vs. Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers et al, NKP 2064 BS, No.9, DN: 7880, P. 1208   Case: Mandamus and directive writ petition regarding the right to privacy of vulnerable groups in judicial proceedings  Plaintiff: Sapana Pradhan Malla representing the Forum for Women, Law and Development (FWLD)  Respondent: Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers (OPM) et al Decision Number: 7880  

This case is related to ensuring the confidentiality and privacy of vulnerable groups, specifically women victims of violence, children, and HIV/AIDS infected individuals from the initial stage of investigation up to final judgment and publication.

  Facts of the Case: The petitioner filed a writ petition seeking protection for the identity and personal details of women victims of violence, children involved in legal disputes and individuals infected with HIV/AIDS during judicial proceedings. The petitioner argued that despite international human rights conventions and constitutional provisions ensuring the right to privacy, Nepal lacked specific legislative measures to keep the identity of these vulnerable groups confidential in legal matters. This exposed them to social stigma, discrimination, and secondary victimization, effectively hindering their access to justice. The respondents (including the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, and the Ministry of Women, Children and Social Welfare) countered that the right to privacy was already a recognized constitutional right. They added that mechanisms like "in-camera" (closed court) hearings already existed under prevailing court regulations and specific acts, meaning additional judicial orders were unnecessary. During the proceedings, Supreme Court requested the petitioner to submit a draft model or procedure detailing how privacy could be maintained. The petitioner subsequently submitted a draft manual to assist the court.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether maintaining confidentiality in legal proceedings infringes upon another party's right to a fair and open trial or violates the public's right to information?
  2. Whether the court possesses the inherent power to order the concealment of personal details of victims and witnesses and whether a directive order should be issued to draft a comprehensive law for this purpose?
  3. Whether it is necessary to issue interim operational guidelines to safeguard privacy until a formal piece of legislation is enacted?
  Decision of the Court: Decision of the Supreme Court: The Supreme Court issued a directive order to the respondents to form a committee comprising relevant stakeholders (including civic bodies and the petitioner organization) to draft a comprehensive bill safeguarding the privacy of these vulnerable classes and present it to the legislature. Recognizing that legislative processes take time, the Court invoked its inherent powers under Article 107(2) of the Interim Constitution of Nepal, 2063. It issued and attached an immediate interim framework titled “विशेष प्रकृतिका मुद्दाहरुको कारवाहीमा पक्षहरुको गोपनीयता कायम राख्ने सम्वन्धी कार्यविधि निर्देशिका, २०६४” (Procedural Guidelines Regarding Maintenance of Privacy of Parties in Special Nature Cases, 2067). The court directed all police stations, government attorney offices, district administrations and courts across Nepal to strictly implement these confidentiality guidelines from the initial FIR/investigation stage till final sentencing and archiving. The Registrar’s Office was mandated to monitor its compliance. Thus, the writ petition was upheld. Principles Established:
  1. If the very private information of an individual is forced to be disclosed except for a specific legal purpose, the individual may not be able to do what he wants with full confidence.
  2. True justice for vulnerable groups (women, children, and HIV/AIDS infected people) requires protecting their personal identity and information from investigation through to the final judgment. Without privacy, fear and social stigma prevent victims from seeking justice.
  3. When it comes to protecting the confidentiality of a child affected by HIV/AIDS, confidentiality may also be required in terms of information of their parents or guardians. Likewise, if a child is raised in prison because his mother is in prison, the information about such upbringing status should also be kept confidential.
  4. Privacy is not just for criminal cases. It also applies to civil cases where revealing a victim's status or identity could cause further harm.
  5. Protecting a victim's identity does not violate the right to an open & fair trial. The accused retains the right to a defense but this must be balanced using special measures (like informal child questioning or video recordings) to protect sensitive witnesses.
  6. The right to information, press, and publication is not absolute; it does not override a victim's right to privacy and justice.
  Relevance of the Case: This landmark verdict revolutionized criminal and civil jurisprudence regarding victim and witness protection. The provided guidelines created the foundation for privacy protocols for Nepal's law enforcement and judicial machinery.

title: Criminology and Penology Case: Advocate Ratna Bahadur Bagchand Vs. Council of Ministers and Others, NKP (5th semester)
content:
Criminology and Penology Case: Advocate Ratna Bahadur Bagchand vs. Council of Ministers and others, Writ No.46/061, NKP 2062 B.S., Decision Date: 2062/01/08, DN 7499   Case: Writ of Mandamus Plaintiff/Applicant: Advocate Ratna Bahadur Bagchand and Others on behalf of Lawyers' National Campaign Against Untouchability (LANCAU) Nepal Defendant/Respondent: Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers and Others Decision Number:7499  

This case is related to caste-based discrimination and untouchability in Nepal.

  Facts of the Case: LANCAU Nepal and its representatives filed a writ petition saying that local authorities had built and operated public drinking water sources separately for Dalits and non-Dalits, thus perpetuating caste based discrimination. They claimed that these practices were in violation of the Constitution of Nepal 2047, the Civil Rights Act, the Water Tax Act, the Local Self-Governance Act, and Nepal's commitment under the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD). The petitioners had asked for a writ of mandamus to be issued to the Government to ensure that the public water sources were available to all irrespective of their caste, to remove the discrimination against the untouchables, and to ensure that the anti-untouchability laws were properly implemented. The respondents rejected the claims and stated that the water facilities were provided on the basis of public convenience and not on caste, that there were already mechanisms and institutions in place to address discrimination, and that the petitioners had not been able to establish any discrimination taking place or use up all other remedies before coming to the Supreme Court.   Legal Issues:
  1. Was there caste-based discrimination in the distribution and use of public drinking water sources?
  2. Should the supreme court issue writ of mandamus?
  3. Is there sufficient evidence to prove such discrimination taking place?
  Different Courts Decisions: Supreme Court: The supreme court did not issue the writ of mandamus as the petitioners were not able to prove, on the basis of facts that discrimination on the basis of caste in public water supply actually occurred in the manner alleged in the petition. The Court also pointed out that the petitioners were not able to show that they had approached competent authorities like the National Dalit Commission for relief beforehand. But the Court noted that the constitutional principle of equality is violated by the practice of untouchability and caste discrimination and that it is in the way of national development, the Court gave a directive order to the Government to take effective steps in the form of awareness and educational programes to eradicate the practice of untouchability and caste discrimination, which is deeply entrenched in society.   Principle Established:
  1. When other remedies are present, before invoking the court’s extraordinary writ jurisdiction the petitioners should exhaust available remedies
  2. Untouchability and caste discrimination is not in line with the fundamental principle of equality guaranteed by the Constitution and it is harmful to social harmony and national development.
  3. The Supreme Court can also give directive orders to the Government even if a writ is rejected so that the Government takes effective steps in the interest of the public.
