title: Criminology and Penology Case: Sunil Babu Panta vs Council of Ministers and others, NKP (5th semester)
content:
Criminology and Penology Case: Sunil Babu Panta vs. Council of Ministers and others, Writ No. 917/064, Date of Decision: 2064/09/06 BS, NKP 2064 B.S, DN: 7958   Case: Public Interest Litigation Plaintiff/Applicant: Sunil Babu Pant, Executive Director of Blue Diamond Society Meena Nepali, Vice Chairperson of MITINI Nepal Sanjeev Gurung, Chairperson of Cruse AIDS Nepal Manoranjan Kumar Vaidya, Executive Director of Parichaya Nepal Defendant/Respondent: Nepal Government, Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers Legislature-Parliament Nepal Government, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Decision Number:7958  

This is a landmark constitutional case which is related to the fundamental rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex (LGBTI) people in Nepal. The Supreme Court's ruling in this case is very progressive, it acknowledged the third-gender identity and declared discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity unconstitutional.

  Facts of the Case: Sunil Babu Pant and four organizations representing around 60000 LGBTI persons in Nepal filed the petition as a Public Interest Litigation. The petitioners contended that sexual and gender minorities faced discrimination, harassment, arbitrary arrests, violence, social exclusion and denial of equal protection of law. The petition also claimed that the Government had denied third gender people citizenship certificates that reflected their gender identity, denied them equal access to education, employment, health care, public services, and other constitutional rights. Current laws were reported to discriminate against LGBTI people and not provide adequate legal protection. The petitioners urged the Court to grant recognition to third gender, remove discriminatory laws and practices, and provide legislation for the rights of sexual and gender minorities, including legal recognition of same sex marriage.   Legal issues:
  • Whether the writ petition could be allowed as a Public Interest Litigation.
  • Whether sexual orientation and gender identity discrimination is a breach of the constitutional right to equality.
  • If homosexuality and transgender identity are natural variations of human identity or mental disorders. The right to third gender status and full constitutional protection.
  Different Courts Decisions: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court said that the petition was maintainable as a valid Public Interest Litigation as it was related to the protection of the fundamental rights of a marginalized community. The Court concluded that sexual orientation and gender identity are natural attributes of the human person and cannot be considered diseases, mental disorders or immoral behavior. All individuals have the right to express and determine their own gender identity and the third gender are natural persons with constitutional rights and legal protection equal to all other citizens. The Court also found that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is a violation of the constitutional rights of equality, dignity, liberty and non-discrimination guaranteed by the Interim Constitution. It recalled that the constitutional rights cannot be disregarded simply on the basis of religious beliefs, social customs, traditions or majority morality. The Court cited international human rights instruments such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) and the Yogyakarta Principles, which it said should be used to interpret the constitution of Nepal. The Supreme Court, therefore, issued the directive order to
  • Accept and respect the third gender identity as a result of self-identification
  • Reconsider and revise all laws and administrative practices that discriminate
  • Promote equal enjoyment of constitutional and legal rights for LGBTI people
  • Respect sexual and gender minorities and prevent discrimination against them
  • Form an expert panel to examine the issue of same sex marriage and suggest suitable laws.
  Principle Established:
  • Public Interest Litigation can be used to safeguard the constitution rights of marginalized groups.
  • Sexual orientation and gender identity are natural and intrinsic attributes of humans, not mental illness
  • Third gender persons have the same constitutional rights, dignity, liberty and legal protection.
  • Discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is unconstitutional.
  • Consensual sexual relations between adults are included in the right to privacy.
  • The State has a positive constitutional obligation to remove discriminatory laws and to achieve substantive equality.
  • International human rights treaties that Nepal has ratified and human rights principles accepted by the international community can be used to interpret the constitutional rights.

title: Criminology and Penology Case: Jeet Kumari Pangeni vs. Council of Ministers and others, NKP (5th semester)
content:
Criminology and Penology Case: Jeet Kumari Pangeni vs. Council of Ministers and others, Writ No. 0035/064, Date of Decision 2060/11/11 B.S, DN:7973   Case: Writ of mandamus Plaintiff/Applicant: Jeet Kumari Pandeni and others Defendant/Respondent: Council of ministers and others Decision Number: 7973  

This case is challenging the constitutionality of the Rape chapter of the Muluki Ain which prescribes only 3-6 months imprisonment in case of marital rape and 5-15 years imprisonment in case of non-marital rape, on the ground that the right to equality has been violated.

  Facts of the Case: Jit Kumari Pangeni was married in 2050 B. S to Bed Prasad Pangeni and had three children. Her husband physically beat her several times after their marriage and insisted on having sex with her without her consent. He allegedly raped and assaulted her even after she refused. She made a criminal complaint to the police and criminal proceedings started. As the case was heard, she found that the current law only gave three to six months imprisonment for marital rape, while rape by anyone else would be punished with five to fifteen years' imprisonment based on the victim's age. The petitioner contended that this distinction was against the married women and infringed their constitutional and human rights. She and women rights activists filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court, asking the court to review the discriminatory provision stating it violated the Interim Constitution's equality provisions, and breached Nepal's obligations under CEDAW, ICCPR, and ICESCR.   Legal issues:
  • Whether prescribing a lower sentence for marital rape is discriminatory and unconstitutional.
  • Whether the Supreme Court should declare the law void, or issue directive order to for harmonization
  Different Courts Decisions: Supreme Court: Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable or constitutional basis for reducing punishment for the victim's husband and that this does not adhere to the equality principle. The Court, however, did not invalidate the provision, but instead issued a directive order to the Government and the Ministry of Law to amend the law and create a punishment in accordance with the constitutional principle of equality. Principle Established:
  • Marital rape is a serious criminal offence and should not be punished less harshly because of the marital relationship.
  • The principle of equality before the law means that the punishment for a crime should be determined by the nature and gravity of the offense and not the relationship between the offender and the victim.
  • While the determination of criminal penalties is the responsibility of the legislature, the Supreme Court can give directive orders when the legislation is not consistent with the constitutional principles.

title: Criminology and Penology Case: Jung Bahadur Singh Vs. Council of Ministers, NKP (5th semester)
content:
Criminology and Penology Case: Jung Bahadur Singh vs. Office of PM and Council of Ministers and others, Writ No. 2066/1222, NKP 2068 B.S, Vol. 6, p. 986, D.N. 8631   Case: writ of certiorari and mandamus Plaintiff/Applicant: Jung Bahadur Singh and others Defendant/Respondent: Council of ministers and others Decision Number: 8631  

This case is related to the fundamental rights of prisoners to reproductive health and reproductive rights as per Interim Constitution of Nepal, 2063. The Supreme Court considered whether the prisoners who are legally married have constitutional rights to family life.

  Facts of the Case: Married couple Surja Marik Dom and Chhotani Devi Marik Dom, who were serving life imprisonment for homicide. The husband and wife were both imprisoned in the same district prison, but were not put in the same prison cell in accordance with prison rules. The couple did not have children before they were imprisoned. They claimed that they would no longer be able to have children as they would lose their natural reproductive capacity before the end of their sentences, thus they would not be able to be a parent again. The petitioners said that Article 20 (2) of the Interim Constitution of Nepal, 2063 gives every woman the right to reproductive health and reproductive rights. They also used constitutional provisions on fundamental rights and Nepal's commitments to international human rights treaties, such as ICCPR and ICESCR. They said that the only right that is suspended by imprisonment is the freedom of movement. Thus, the refusal of married prisoners to have the opportunity to live in a family and exercise reproductive rights infringed their fundamental rights. The Government disagreed, stating that all constitutional rights could not be exercised in the same way by prisoners as free citizens who had been convicted of serious offences. It also argued that the current prison legislation did not include provisions for conjugal visits, and that the decision making process was the sole prerogative of the executive. In the light of the provisions of the Constitution, prison law, international human rights law and comparative international law, the Supreme Court decided that reproductive rights are fundamental rights even while the person is imprisoned and that the State has a duty to protect those rights subject to reasonable security measures.   Legal issues:
  1. The issue of prisoner’s constitutional right to reproductive health and reproductive rights while in custody.
  2. Does it infringe the fundamental rights of the prisoners, guaranteed under Interim Constitution of Nepal, 2063, to keep them in different cells of the prison without allowing any family visit?
  3. Whether the imprisonment suspends all the constitutional rights of a prisoner or only the right to personal liberty and movement.
  Different Courts Decisions: Supreme Court: The Court ruled that all fundamental rights are not suspended by the imposition of a sentence of imprisonment. It concluded that the prisoners, who are legally married, have the right to reproduction as guaranteed by the Constitution and ordered the Government to set up a committee, draw up suitable legislation and policy, and gradually implement a system of family (conjugal) visits for prisoners who are legally married, with due consideration to the security and discipline of prisons.   Principle Established:
  • Imprisonment does not suspend all fundamental rights.
  • Reproductive rights are fundamental rights and apply even to convicted prisoners.
  • Prisoners should be treated with dignity and given opportunities for rehabilitation and social reintegration
  • International human rights instruments can be used as a guide for constitutional interpretation.

title: Criminology and Penology Case: Prakash Mani Sharma V. Council of Ministers and others, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Criminology and Penology Case: Prakash Mani Sharma vs. Council of Ministers and others, NKP 2065 B.S, Vol 4. D.N. 7952   Case: Sexual Rights of Pregnant Women Prisoners Plaintiff/Applicant: Advocate Prakash Mani Sharma & Others Defendant/Respondent: Council of Ministers & Others Decision Number:7952  

The case is about the constitutional challenges to the provisions of the Prison Act, 2019 which barred certain categories of pregnant women prisoners from being released on bail on the basis of the gravity of their offence.

  Facts of the Case: Section 12(1) of the Prison Act, 2019 was challenged in a PIL by Janahit Sanrakshan Manch (Pro Public) and Advocate Prakash Mani Sharma. The provision was that a pregnant woman prisoner could be released on bail after six months of pregnancy, but not those convicted or charged with offences like murder, life imprisonment, offences against the State or offences involving the royal family. The petitioners argued that such a distinction is unfair to pregnant women prisoners and infringes upon the constitutional right to equality. They also argued that the State had failed to provide adequate health care, nutrition, and facilities for pregnant prisoners and their dependent children, and requested the Court to formulate national standards and direct the government to improve prison conditions.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether Section 12(1) of Prison Act, 2019 infringed the constitutional right to equality by discriminating against the pregnant prisoners on the basis of the nature of their offences.
  2. Whether it was unconstitutional for the government to exclude prisoners convicted of serious offences from temporary release.
  3. Whether the Government should be directed to frame proper policies and minimum standards for the protection, health, nutrition and welfare of pregnant women prisoners and their children.
  Different Courts Decisions: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge to the constitutionality of Section 12(1) and held that classification of prisoners based on the seriousness of the offences was a reasonable and permissible classification and did not violate the constitutional right to equality. The Court has held that equality involves treating like cases alike and that unlike cases can be treated differently if there is a rational basis. The Court, however, noted that the Government has failed to address the plight of pregnant prisoners and issued a directive order to the Government to formulate and implement policies and programmes to provide proper health care, nutrition, protection and other necessary facilities to pregnant prisoners, breastfeeding mothers and their children.   Principle Established:
  • Under the Constitution, reasonable classification is allowed if it is rationally related to a legitimate purpose.
  • The classification of criminal offences, according to the seriousness of the offence, is constitutionally valid and not discriminatory provided it meets the test of reasonableness.
  • Pregnant women convicted of serious offences are not in the same category as pregnant women convicted of ordinary offences for the purposes of temporary release.
  • Even if the restriction on release is constitutionally valid, the State has an ongoing responsibility to provide adequate health care, nutrition and protection for pregnant women prisoners and their dependent children.

title: Criminology and Penology Case: HMG Vs. Samjhana Lamichhane, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Criminology and Penology Case: HMG vs. Samjhana Lamichhane, NKP 2060 B.S, P 77, D.N. 7169   Case: Infanticide Plaintiff/Applicant: HMG Defendant/Respondent: Samjhana Lamichhane Decision Number: 7169  

This case is about the murder of a baby (infanticide).

  Facts of the Case: Samjhana Lamichhane Dhakal got pregnant as a result of an illegal relationship with her brother-in-law Manoj Mukhiya. She kept the pregnancy a secret from her family, even from her own mother, to avoid social stigma and disgrace. She secretly gave birth at home without informing anyone on 31 Shrawan 2058 B.S. Police lodged a report after the body of a newborn baby was found. In the course of the inspection, the police discovered a wound on the right temple of the baby's head which was about two inches long and looked suspicious. The accused first made a statement to the investigating officer that the baby fell to the ground during childbirth and died as a result. She has said that she did not mean to kill the child. She told the court that she did not kill the baby and that the child fell to the ground when she was in great pain and briefly unconscious. The investigation, however, found that there were no stones or objects at the place of birth which could have caused the injury described by the accused. It was also revealed that upon the child's birth, she wrapped her body and took it to a field below the house, where she hid it from others. From the physical evidence, the concealment of the pregnancy and body and the circumstances, the prosecution drew the conclusion that the child was born alive and that the accused had intended to kill the child to prevent social stigma.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the prosecution has established on a reasonable doubt standard that the accused killed the newborn child intentionally and in fact.
  2. Whether the accused had committed the offence under Chapter on Homicide, Sections 1 and 13(3) of the Muluki Ain.
  3. Reducing the mandatory punishment of life imprisonment with confiscation of property, taking into account the age, social background and circumstances of the accused in the context of No. 188 of the Chapter on Court Procedure.
  Different Courts Decisions: District Court: Gorkha District Court found that the prosecution had established beyond reasonable doubt that Samjhana Lamichhane Dhakal killed her newborn child on purpose. Under Sections 1 and 13(3) of the Chapter on Homicide of the Muluki Ain, it found her guilty which prescribes life imprisonment with confiscation of property. The Court, however, noted that the accused was only about 18-19 years old, that she committed the offence to hide the illegitimate pregnancy and to avoid social disgrace and that she did not use any deadly weapon to commit the offence, and therefore, the Court considered the statutory punishment as too harsh. Exercising its power under No. 188 of the Chapter on Court Procedure, it recommended that her sentence be reduced to five years imprisonment instead of life imprisonment. Appellate Court: Pokhara Appellate Court upheld the District Court's decision and agreed that the prosecution had established the offence of murder. It had concluded that the accused was legally liable to the punishment provided in Section 13(3) which was life imprisonment with confiscation of property. However, it agreed that this would be too harsh taking into consideration the age of the accused and the context of the offence. Therefore, it accepted the recommendation of the District Court to impose five years imprisonment and remanded it to the Supreme Court for confirmation of sentence (Sadhak review). Supreme Court: On a careful scrutiny of the evidence on record, the Supreme Court confirmed the conviction. It concluded that the accused had intentionally concealed her pregnancy from everyone, given birth to the child without informing anyone, and intentionally killed the child. Her defence of accidental death after the child fell onto stones during childbirth was rejected as there were no stones found at the place of delivery. It also took the injury on the baby's head, the concealment of the pregnancy and the accused's act of wrapping the baby up in cloth and hiding it in a nearby field as strong circumstantial evidence that she was guilty beyond reasonable doubt. Supreme Court accepted that the offence was one which attracted life imprisonment with confiscation of property but it found that even the lesser sentence of five years imprisonment recommended by the lower courts was too harsh. Considering the accused's tender age, the background of the offence, the social stigma attached to an out of wedlock pregnancy and the social situation, the Court found that the time already served by the accused was adequate to secure the ends of justice. It thus shortened her sentence to what she had already served and ordered her immediate release.   Principle Established:
  • When all the circumstances point to the accused and there is no direct evidence, circumstantial evidence may be enough to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
  • The concealment of pregnancy, secret childbirth, concealment of the body and false explanations may all constitute a criminal intent.
  • Young age, social and societal pressures are relevant mitigating factors in sentencing the offender.
  • The aim of sentencing is not just punishment but also justice that is proportionate with the circumstance of the offence.

title: Criminology and Penology Case: Shanti B.K. vs. HMG, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Criminology and Penology Case: Shanti B.K. vs. HMG, NKP 2061 B.S, DN 7399   Case: Infanticide Plaintiff/Applicant: HMG Defendant/Respondent: Shanti B.K Decision Number: 7399  

This is a case of a woman killing her newborn child following an out of wedlock pregnancy. 

    Facts of the Case: Shanti B.K.'s husband had gone to India for employment. She got intimate with Narayan Bahadur B.K. while he was away, and got pregnant. She told Narayan Bahadur about the pregnancy, and asked him to accept her, but he refused and told her to kill the child after it was born. She was distressed at his refusal and abandoned by both the family of her husband and her family, and was afraid of social shame, so she secretly gave birth to a baby boy at her home. Her statement to the police and the court was that the child was born alive. She hit the baby several times with her fists on his face and head until she thought he was dead. Then she wrapped the body in cloth, took it to a place named Rahegaira and buried it in a dug pit. Her father-in-law complained and the police found the baby's body. The post mortem examination showed the child had died from asphyxia causing brain damage and a medical examination revealed that Shanti had recently given birth. She later appealed saying that the child was stillborn and that her confession was given under police pressure, but the medical evidence, her previous confessions and other evidence did not support her defense.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the prosecution was able to establish that the accused intentionally killed her child?
  2. Whether the accused had the right to a reduced sentence pursuant to No. 188 of the Chapter on Court Procedure?
  3. What should be the principles that guide the court in exercising its judicial discretion to mitigate punishment?
  Different Courts Decisions: District Court: Palpa District Court found that the prosecution had established that Shanti B.K. had killed her baby intentionally. It was based on her confession to the police and court, medical evidence that the baby was born alive and died of asphyxia, and the evidence of witnesses. For this reason, it found her guilty of the offences under Sections 1 and 13(3) of the Chapter on Homicide, for which the prescribed punishment was life imprisonment and confiscation of property. Yet, as a young woman, whose husband was away from home, and who was abandoned after falling pregnant from an extra marital affair, the District Court felt the statutory punishment was too harsh as it was not committed with premeditated malice. Accordingly, it recommended, under No. 188 of the Chapter on Court Procedure, that her sentence be reduced to five years' imprisonment. High court: Butwal Appellate Court rejected the appeal filed by the accused and upheld the District Court's verdict that the accused had intentionally killed her newborn child. The Court concluded that the confession, medical reports, witness statements and circumstances surrounding her case proved she was guilty beyond reasonable doubt. It also agreed that the statutory punishment of life imprisonment with the confiscation of property would be unduly severe in the circumstances in which the offence was committed. It thus accepted the District Court's recommendation that the sentence be reduced to five years' imprisonment and sent the matter back to the Supreme Court for (Sadhak). Supreme Court: Supreme Court upheld the conviction, finding that the evidence was sufficient to prove that Shanti B.K. had intentionally killed her newborn child and buried the body. The Court did not accept her subsequent contention that the child was stillborn and that her confession was coerced, since her pre-investigation and pre-court statements were consistent and corroborated by the medical evidence of death by asphyxia and the evidence of a recent delivery. Thus, the conviction under Section 13(3) of the Chapter on Homicide was upheld. The Supreme Court then reviewed the sentence reduction recommended in No. 188. The Court used the occasion to establish important guidelines on sentencing, which include the following: Sentences must be imposed on the basis of clear and consistent standards; and similarly situated offenders must be punished in the same manner. It said that the judge should take into account the circumstances of the offence, the intention of the offender, his age, social background, physical and mental state, family situation, remorse, cooperation with the judicial process, influence or pressure exerted by others, and whether the offence was deliberate or not, when exercising his discretion in No. 188. The Court, applying these principles, found that the accused had confessed to the offence, had cooperated with the court, had not planned the act, had no personal animosity towards the child's father, had been emotionally distressed after being abandoned by the child's father, had no support from her marital family or her own family, and had committed the offence under intense social pressure to avoid the stigma of an illegitimate pregnancy. In such unusual cases, the Court deemed that life imprisonment would be unduly severe. It thus accepted the recommendations of both the lower courts and imposed a term of five years imprisonment instead of life imprisonment with confiscation of property.   Principle Established:
  • Sentencing should be based on clear, rational and consistent principles, ensuring that offenders in similar situations receive similar sentences.
  • 188 of the Chapter on Court Procedure requires that the judge be cautious in imposing a lesser sentence and that there be identifiable mitigating circumstances. Some of the factors that are taken into account in sentencing are the offender's intent, motive, age, social background, family circumstances, physical health, mental health, degree of remorse, cooperation with the judicial system, influence or pressure from others, and whether the offense was premeditated.
  • Voluntary confession with reliable medical and circumstantial evidence may be used to prove murder.
  • Murder normally carries a life sentence, but where mitigation is warranted by the interests of justice, it is possible for a substantial sentence reduction to be ordered.

title: Taxation Law Case: Tax Office Biratnagar vs. Mahendra Kumar Golchha, NKP(9th  Semester)
content:
Taxation Law Case: Tax Office Biratnagar vs. Mahendra Kumar Golchha, NKP (2063 B.S.), No. 7,  P. 871,  DN. 7730     Case: Income Tax Plaintiff: Finance Ministry, Inland Revenue Department, Tax Office Biratnagar Defendant: Hulas Wire Industries Pvt. Ltd. founder Mahendra Kumar Golchha Decision Number: 7730  

This case is related to the dispute of income tax

  Facts of the Case: The case arose from an income tax dispute between Hulas Wire Industries (Pvt.) Ltd. and the Tax Office, Biratnagar, concerning the company's income tax assessment for the fiscal year 2050/51 B.S. Hulas Wire Industries submitted its self-assessment income tax return on 1 Poush 2051 B.S., declaring its net profit and calculating its tax liability in accordance with the Income Tax Act, 2031. Under the self-assessment system, the company was responsible for preparing and submitting its own tax return based on its financial records. After receiving the return, Tax Office conducted an examination of the company's accounts and financial transactions. During this process, it recorded the statement of the company's representative and issued a notice under Section 33(4) of the Income Tax Act, directing the company to submit supporting documents and evidence for the expenses claimed in its tax return. The company complied by producing its books of accounts, vouchers, financial statements, audit report, and other relevant documents in support of its claims. Upon reviewing the records, the Tax Office concluded that several expenses claimed by the company could not be deducted while computing taxable income. These included certain repair and maintenance expenses, vehicle operating and repair costs, sales depot expenses, and salary-related expenses. The Tax Office considered these expenses either inadmissible or insufficiently supported and added them back to the company's taxable income. As a result, it determined the company's net taxable income at Rs. 53,23,492.49/-. Based on this reassessment, the Tax Office issued an income tax assessment order requiring Hulas Wire Industries to pay Rs. 15,05,892.46/- which included Rs. 13,07,995.75/- as outstanding income tax after adjustment of advance tax and Rs. 1,97,896.71/- as a penalty. The company was directed to deposit the amount within thirty-five days. The company challenged the assessment before the Revenue Tribunal, Biratnagar, arguing that the Tax Office had wrongly disallowed genuine business expenses that were incurred wholly and exclusively for business purposes. It also contended that although tax had initially not been deducted from some employees' salaries due to an oversight, the required tax had later been deducted and deposited with the bank, and therefore those salary expenses should not have been added to taxable income. After examining the evidence, including payment vouchers and tax deduction records, the Revenue Tribunal held that some of the disputed expenses were legitimate business expenses and should have been allowed as deductions. It found that the company had produced sufficient proof regarding tax deduction on employees' salaries and that certain sales depot expenses and other operating expenses had been wrongly disallowed. Accordingly, the Tribunal partly reversed the tax assessment order issued by the Tax Office. Dissatisfied with the Tribunal's decision, the Tax Office, Biratnagar, sought leave to appeal before the Supreme Court. It argued that the Tribunal had incorrectly interpreted the provisions of the Income Tax Act and had failed to properly appreciate the evidence on record. The Supreme Court granted leave to appeal and examined whether the Tribunal had correctly allowed the disputed deductions and whether the Tax Office had justified its decision to treat those expenses as taxable income.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the Revenue Tribunal was justified in allowing the deduction of repair and maintenance expenses, vehicle repair expenses, and sales depot expenses while computing the taxable income of Hulas Wire Industries?
  2. Whether the salary expenses, where tax had initially not been deducted at source but was subsequently deducted and deposited, could still be treated as deductible business expenses or should be added back to the company's taxable income?
  3. Whether the Tax Office had discharged its legal burden of proving that the disputed expenses were capital or otherwise non-deductible, thereby justifying the reassessment of the company's taxable income and the partial reversal of the Tribunal's decision?
  Decisions of the Court: Tax office, Biratnagar: It disallowed repair and maintenance expenses by treating them as capital expenditure and disallowed sales depot expenses. It added salary payments to taxable income because tax had not been deducted at source at the time of payment. Similarly, it increased the taxpayer's taxable income and imposed additional tax and penalties.   Revenue Tribunal, Biratnagar: It held that the repair and maintenance expenses were legitimate business expenses and deductible. The sales depot expenses were allowable despite there being no sales during the year because maintaining the depot required unavoidable operational expenses. It accepted evidence showing that TDS had subsequently been deducted and deposited. Lastly, it reversed the Tax Office's decision regarding these items.   Supreme Court: Dismissed the Tax Office's appeal and upheld the decision of the Revenue Tribunal. It held that the Tax Office failed to prove why the repair expenses were capital in nature. It confirmed that genuine business expenses remain deductible even if they do not generate income in that year. It also held that subsequent lawful deposit of TDS cured the earlier omission. And lastly, it emphasized that tax authorities must justify tax assessments with evidence and legal reasoning.   Established principles: The tax officer's tax assessment function is a judicial function. Since the tax officer is the investigating officer in the tax assessment process as well as the tax assessor, his legal status is both that of an accused and a decision maker. In a tax dispute, where the taxpayer shows that a certain amount is not taxable for any reason, the tax officer or office wishing to impose tax must show that it is taxable under this provision. The burden of proving that it is taxable income lies with the tax office or tax officer. Since the burden of proof is of utmost importance and necessity in tax-related disputes, the burden of proof should not be solely on the taxpayer. Since it is found that the taxpayer has deducted the amount at source as per the law by mistake and later paid it, the decision of the Revenue Tribunal that the amount should not be included in the personal income cannot be said to have violated the law, and the order granting permission cannot be agreed with as it appears to be justified.   Relevancy of the Case: This case is highly relevant in the field of tax law as it clarifies the principles governing the deductibility of business expenses and the burden of proof in tax assessments. The Supreme Court affirmed that genuine business expenses incurred in the ordinary course of business cannot be disallowed without sufficient legal and factual justification, and that the Tax Office must establish why an expense is capital or otherwise non-deductible. The decision also recognizes that procedural errors, such as delayed deduction of tax at source, may be rectified in accordance with the law without automatically denying legitimate deductions. Consequently, this case serves as an important precedent for ensuring fairness, reasoned decision-making, and the protection of taxpayers' rights in income tax assessments.

title: Taxation Law Case: Laxman Narayan vs. Tax Office Lalitpur, NKP (9th Semester)
content:
Taxation Law Case: Laxman  Narayan vs. Tax  Office  Lalitpur,  NKP (2064 B.S), No. 6, P.  758.,  D. N. 7859   Case: Income Tax Plaintiff: Laxman Narayan Shrestha Defendant: Government of Nepal, Ministry of Finance, Inland Revenue Office, Lalitpur Decision Number: 7859  

This case is related to dispute of income tax

  Facts of the Case: The dispute arose from the income tax assessment of Hotel Himalaya Pvt. Ltd. for the fiscal year 2053/54. The hotel filed its self-assessment return showing a taxable income of Rs. 60,33,455.61/- and calculated its income tax at the concessional rate of 20% under the amended Industrial Enterprises Act, 2049, which had reduced the tax rate for eligible industries. The hotel had already deposited Rs. 17,11,886.99/- as advance tax and claimed that its self-assessment was in accordance with the law because the amended tax rate was in force at the end of the income year. The Tax Office, Lalitpur, did not accept the hotel's calculation. Instead, it divided the income year into two periods. It applied the old tax rate of 28% for the period before 27 Jestha 2054, when the amendment came into force, and the reduced rate of 20% for the remaining part of the year. On that basis, it determined the total tax liability at Rs. 16,40,438.72/- and decided that the excess advance tax paid by the hotel would be adjusted in the following fiscal year. The Revenue Tribunal upheld this decision, holding that the reduced rate could only apply from the date the amendment became effective and not to the earlier part of the same income year. The hotel challenged the Tribunal's decision before the Supreme Court. It argued that under Section 4 of the Income Tax Act, 2031, income tax for a fiscal year must be assessed using the tax rate in force on the last day of the income year, not by splitting the year into different periods with different tax rates. The hotel maintained that because the 20% rate was in force on the last day of the fiscal year, the entire income of that year should be taxed at 20%. The Supreme Court agreed with this argument, holding that income tax is an annual tax and that a taxpayer carrying on business throughout the year cannot be subjected to two different tax rates for the same income year. Accordingly, it set aside the Tribunal's decision to the extent it applied the 28% rate and held that the hotel's income for the fiscal year 2053/54 was taxable entirely at the rate of 20%.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the income tax for the fiscal year 2053/54 should be calculated at the single tax rate of 20% that was in force on the last day of the income year, or by applying two different tax rates (28% and 20%) to different periods of the same year?
  2. Whether the Tax Office and the Revenue Tribunal were legally justified in dividing one income year into two parts and assessing income tax at different rates after the amendment to the Industrial Enterprises Act came into force?
  3. Whether, under Section 4 of the Income Tax Act, 2031, a taxpayer carrying on business throughout the year can be subjected to more than one income tax rate for the same income year?
    Decisions of the Court: Tax Office, Lalitpur: The Tax Office rejected the hotel's self-assessment. It held that the reduced 20% tax rate introduced by the amendment could apply only from 27 Jestha 2054, the date the amendment came into force. Accordingly, it applied the earlier rate of 28% to the period before the amendment and 20% to the remaining part of the fiscal year. On this basis, it calculated the hotel's tax liability at Rs. 16,40,438.72/- and decided that the excess advance tax paid would be adjusted in the next fiscal year.   Revenue Tribunal, Kathmandu: The Revenue Tribunal upheld the Tax Office's decision. It reasoned that since the amendment reducing the tax rate became effective only on 27 Jestha 2054, it could not be given retrospective effect for the earlier part of the fiscal year. Therefore, the Tribunal found that applying two different tax rates to two different periods of the same income year was lawful and dismissed the hotel's appeal   Supreme Court: Supreme Court reversed the decisions of the Tax Office and the Revenue Tribunal. It held that income tax is an annual tax, and under Section 4 of the Income Tax Act, 2031, the applicable tax rate is the rate in force on the last day of the income year. Since the 20% rate was effective on the last day of the fiscal year 2053/54, the entire income of that year had to be taxed at 20%. The Court further ruled that a taxpayer carrying on business throughout the year cannot be subjected to two different tax rates for the same income year and directed that the hotel's tax be recalculated at the uniform rate of 20%, with any excess tax paid to be refunded in accordance with the law.   Established Principles: If, after calculating a taxpayer's income and expenses for the entire fiscal year in accordance with the law at the end of that year, a profit is found, that profit is regarded as the taxpayer's income for that year. The applicable tax rate is determined in accordance with the tax rate in force on the last day of the income year, as provided under Section 4 of the Income Tax Act, 2031. Except in the case of occasional or isolated transactions that generate income, income tax is always levied on the income earned over a complete year. Therefore, for income tax purposes, the full fiscal year serves as the basis for taxation. However, in relation to certain types of income arising under specific circumstances, the law may provide that income tax is imposed at the time the income is earned. Since the applicable income tax rate is the rate in force at the end of the income year, even if the law amends the income tax rate several times during that year, the taxpayer's income tax must be assessed using the rate in force on the last day of the income year, i.e., the last day of Ashadh (mid-July). Income tax is always assessed after determining the profit or loss by accounting for all business transactions, receipts, and expenditures of the preceding year in the following year. This also justifies applying the tax rate that is in force at the end of the income year. Therefore, for taxpayers engaged in continuous business throughout the year, there can never be more than one applicable income tax rate for that 8 year.

title: Intellectual Property Case: Mihir Kumar Thakur vs. Bhesh Jung Badal Lamichhane, NKP (6th Semester)
content:
Intellectual Property Case: Mihir Kumar Thakur vs. Bhesh Jung Badal Lamichhane, NKP 2066 B.S, Number 12, p. 2017, DN 8283   Case: Writ Petition regarding validity of service of summons Plaintiff/Applicant: Mihir Kumar Thakur Defendant/Respondent: Bhesh Jung Badal Lamichhane Decision Number: 8283  

This case is related to Copyright Law and Civil Procedure.

  Facts of the Case: The petitioner, a former law professor, authored a Nepali book titled “Nepali Sambidhan ra Rajniti - Nirnayak Ghatana ra Mod”, for which he held registered copyright. He filed a complaint alleging that the respondent, Bhesh Jung Badal, published an unauthorized English translation titled “The King Versus The People”, infringing his copyright. A copyright infringement case was filed at Kathmandu District Court. The respondent went into hiding and never showed up for this case. While avoiding the copyright case, the respondent turned around and filed a separate defamation case against the petitioner over a newspaper article about the copyright dispute. Oddly, he showed up and actively fought this case, even though it was heard together with the case he was “avoiding.” The District Court decided both cases and the respondent was found guilty of copyright infringement and ordered to pay compensation and his defamation claim against the petitioner failed. Nobody appealed, so this decision became final. When the petitioner tried to enforce the judgement and collect compensation, the respondent suddenly claimed - nearly seven months later - that he had never been properly notified of the original copyright case, and asked the court to cancel that notice and let him restart his defense. The District Court rejected this saying that the notice had been properly served. The respondent then appealed to the Patan Appellate Court which reopened the case and later the petitioner approached the Supreme Court arguing this reopening was not legally justified.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the Patan Appellate Court’s order declaring the summons served on the respondent was lawful.
  2. Whether the writ of certiorari (and mandamus) sought by the petitioner should be issued.
  3. Whether a defendant who had actual knowledge of the case can still claim the benefit.
  Different Courts Decision: Kathmandu District Court: District Court held the service of summons was proper and rejected the respondent’s application. Patan Appellate Court: Appellate Court annulled the summons as defective - based on a ward committee’s recommendation that the witnesses were not actual residents of the ward - and ordered the District Court to proceed lawfully. Supreme Court: Supreme Court held that the Appellate Court erred by relying on material outside the case record and outside the scope of what was before the trial court when the original order was made. It found that the respondent had actual knowledge of the copyright case which is evidenced by his simultaneous, active pursuit of a related defamation case concerning the very same subject matter. The Court concluded that the respondent’s claim was made in bad faith to delay execution of a final judgement. The Court issued an order of certiorari quashing the Patan Appellate Court’s order and all consequent proceedings. The Court also issued a writ of mandamus directing Kathmandu District Court to proceed with enforcement of its judgment.   Principle Established:
  1. When determining whether service of summons was proper or defective under No. 17 of the Court Proceedings, the Appellate Court must confine itself to material that was part of the original case record and it cannot rely on recommendations or facts introduced only after the petition was filed.
  2. The duty of a notice-issuing authority is to make an honest, good-faith effort to communicate notice to the concerned person; the doctrine of notice cannot be used to satisfy a party who denies receiving notice or feigns ignorance despite having received it. Otherwise, service of summons becomes a mere ritualistic, mechanical formality.
  3. A party who had knowledge of a case cannot later claim ignorance to invoke the relief.

title: Interpretation of Law Case: Kanchha Prajapati vs. Nhechchhe Kumar Prajapati, NKP (6th Semester)
content:
Interpretation of Law Case: Kanchha Prajapati vs. Nhuchche Kumar Prajapati, NKP 2048 B.S, Vol: 9, DN: 4350. Case: Writ of Certiorari Plaintiff: Nhuchhe Kumar Prajapati et al. Respondent: Kancha Prajapati Decision Number: 4350  

This case is related to the transfer of tenancy rights (Mohiyani Hak) and the statutory interpretation of the word “son” regarding inheritance.

Facts of the Case: A plot of Guthi (trust) land in Bhaktapur, was registered under the name of Chandravir Kumar Prajapati. This trust was managed by a group of 62 trustees (Guthiyars). The registered tenant (Mohi) cultivating the specific plot of land was Mahila Prajapati. Following the death of the registered owner, Chandravir Kumar Prajapati, the remaining trustees, including the petitioner Nhuchhe Kumar Prajapati, submitted an application to the Land Revenue Office in Bhaktapur. They successfully transferred the land ownership into their names and were issued a joint land ownership certificate. Meanwhile, having no wife or any biological children, Mahila formally adopted a minor, Ram Bahadur Prajapati, on 2041/11/14 B.S., to continue his lineage, and died shortly after, on 2042/5/4 B.S. As Ram Bahadur was a minor, his guardian and uncle, Kanchha Prajapati, applied to the Land Reform Office (LRO) in Bhaktapur to transfer the tenancy rights to the adopted son’s name. Relying on the Nepal Law Interpretation Act, 2010, which defines “son” to include an adopted son, the officer at LRO approved the transfer without consulting the landowners. However, the officer made this decision unilaterally, without issuing a notice to, or seeking a response from, the registered landowners. The guthiyars group, led by Nhuchhe Kumar Prajapati, filed a writ petition challenging this decision Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the term “son” used in Section 26 (1) of the Lands Act, 2021 B.S., legally encompasses an adopted son (Dharmaputra).
  2. Whether an adopted son is legally entitled to inherit the tenancy rights (Mohiyani Hak) of his deceased adoptive father.
  3. Whether the general definitions provided in the Nepal Law Interpretation Act, 2010 B.S. should be applied to interpret undefined terms in specific statutes like the Lands Act.
Decision of the Court: Supreme Court: While the Joint Bench initially ruled against the respondent, the Full Bench of the Supreme Court, upon review, reversed that very decision and upheld the Land Reform Office’s Orders, transferring the tenancy right to the adopted son. The court stated that, as per Section 2(c) of the Nepal Interpretation of Laws Act, 2010 B.S., the legal definition of “son” clearly includes an adopted son as well. Since the Lands Act does not provide a conflicting definition, there is no legal reason or basis to restrict the meaning to only ‘biological sons’. Moreover, it further ruled that the Joint Bench had erred in considering the earlier ruling in Sheshnath Prasad Kurmi precedent as a legal misinterpretation, for under the Act, the Land Reform Officer had jurisdiction to record tenancy in the name of an adopted son. The Court set aside these orders and reinstated the transfer of tenancy rights to Ram Bahadur Prajapati. Thus, the court established that an adopted son has full rights to inherit the tenancy.   Principles Established:
  1. When a term is defined under the Nepal Interpretation of Laws Act, 2010 B.S., the definition provided by the said Act applies, unless a different meaning is given under another law.
  2. As per the principle of interpretation, when the language of a statute is clear and unambiguous, courts must give it its ordinary legal meaning and should not adopt an artificial or restrictive interpretation.
  3. For Section 26(1) of the Lands Act, the term “son” includes an adopted son, as the Act contains no provision excluding adopted sons.
  4. Courts should adopt a liberal and purposive interpretation of statutes to uphold legal rights and achieve justice, rather than a narrow or restrictive interpretation.
  5. The earlier principle established in Sheshnath Prasad Kurmi v. Land Reform Office, Parsa (NKP Vol. 29, No. 2, p. 140), which held that the term “son” in the Lands Act did not include an adopted son, thereby denying adopted sons the right to inherit tenancy, was overruled.
  Relevance of the Case: This case is a landmark precedent in the interpretation of statutes in Nepal. It establishes that statutory terms must be interpreted according to the Nepal Law Interpretation Act unless the concerned law provides otherwise, and that courts should adopt a liberal interpretation to uphold justice.
rationale: Title clearly represents distinct academic subject (Interpretation of Law) absent from Prisma.

title: Interpretation of Law Case: Lok Bhakta Rana vs. Rama Devi, NKP (6th Semester)
content:
Interpretation of Law Case: Rama Devi Rajbhandari vs. Lok Bhakta Shumsher J.B.R., NKP 2055 B.S, Vol: 11, DN: 6625.   Case: Forgery of Documents Plaintiff: Rama Devi Rajbhandari Respondent: Lok Bhakta Shumsher J.B.R Decision Number: 6625  

This case is related to the interpretation of statutes, decided in the context of forgery and the statute of limitations for filing such cases.

Facts of the Case: The case concerned about 1 Ropani and 1 Aana of land at Tankeshwor, Tahachal. Rama Devi Rajbhandari claimed that the land had been gifted to her through a registered deed of gift (Bakaspatra) and that she was in possession of it. Later, Sungabha Gurungseni executed a registered relinquishment deed (Chhodpatra) transferring the same land to Lokbhakta Shamsher J.B.R. Rama Devi claimed that this deed was forged because the land had already been gifted to her. She therefore filed a case seeking punishment for forgery and cancellation of the disputed deed. The defendants denied the forgery and argued that the case was filed after the two-year limitation period prescribed for forgery cases under the Muluki Ain, 2020 B.S. The main dispute before the Court was therefore whether the deed was forged and whether the case was filed within the required limitation period. Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the limitation period for a forgery case starts from the date of the forged deed or the date when the forgery was discovered.
  2. Whether the Court can depart from the clear and literal meaning of the law on grounds of fairness or equity, without interfering with the legislature’s role.
  3. Whether the plaintiff’s case, filed about six years after the disputed deed, was barred by limitation.
Different Courts Decisions: Bagmati Zonal Court: The court dismissed the case as time-barred, holding that it was filed after the two-year limitation period prescribed under No. 18 of the Chapter on Forgery of the Muluki Ain had expired. Central Regional Court (Appellate Court): It upheld the Bagmati Zonal Court’s decision, holding that the case was time-barred because it was not filed within two years from the date of the alleged forgery. Supreme Court: The Joint Bench of the Supreme Court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiff, disagreeing with the lower courts’ view that the case was time-barred. The case was later reviewed by a Special Bench, which overturned the Joint Bench’s decision and dismissed the plaintiff’s case. The Special Bench held that the law clearly required a forgery case to be filed within two years from the date the forgery was committed. Since the wording of the law was clear, the Court held that it could not interpret it as starting from the date of discovery.   Principles Established:
  1. When the language of a statute provides a plain, clear, and straightforward meaning, there is no room for judicial interpretation. The court must apply the law exactly as it is written, without altering its words.  
  2.  If a law is inadequate, incomplete, or creates practical difficulties, it is the sole responsibility of the legislature to amend it. The court cannot rewrite or create new laws under the guise of interpretation, as doing so falls outside its judicial jurisdiction. 
  3. Interpreting a clear legal provision based on emotional grounds, logical assumptions, or personal convenience destroys the true intent of the legislature. Active legislation must be strictly respected and followed by the courts.  
  4. Clear statutory words on limitation cannot be changed by judicial interpretation. Interpreting “the date the act was committed” as “the date of discovery” would go against the law and amount to unauthorized judicial law-making.

title: Interpretation of Laws Case: K.I. Singh vs. His Majesty’s Government of Nepal, NKP (6th Semester)
content:
Interpretation of Law Case: Dr. K.I. Singh vs. His Majesty’s Government of Nepal, NKP 2022 B.S, Vol: 3, DN: 279. Case: Offenses Against the State (Causing Hatred, Malice and Contempt) Plaintiff: His Majesty’s Government Respondent: Ex PM Dr. K.I. Singh and Keshav Chandra Gautam Decision Number: 279  

This case is related to offences against the State and the interpretation of legislative intent in determining whether public criticism of the Government falls within the offence of creating hatred, malice and contempt against the State.

  Facts of the Case: The government authorities searched the residence of former Prime Minister Dr. K.I. Singh on Falgun 26, 2020 B.S., during which they found and seized press statements as well as printed pamphlets that called for a “nationwide non-violent satyagraha” (civil disobedience movement). The pamphlets had criticized the Government for violating democratic principles, raised several political demands, and called upon the public to join a peaceful collective movement. Likewise, On Falgun 30, 2020 B.S., coinciding with Ghode Jatra, Dr. Singh publicly distributed the pamphlets and delivered a speech at Bhugol Park, Kathmandu. He later confirmed these actions in a written statement. Co-defendant Keshav Chandra Gautam also distributed the pamphlets and delivered a supporting speech, endorsing Dr. Singh’s statements and political demands. Following these activities, the Government initiated legal proceedings against both individuals, alleging that their speeches and distribution of pamphlets were intended to create hatred, malice, and contempt against the Government under Section 6 of the Rajkaj (Offences and Punishments) Act, 2019. In his defense, Dr. Singh stated that his actions were an exercise of peaceful political expression intended to pressure the Government for policy reform, and that a call for non-violent movement was not equivalent to inciting hatred or sedition against the State.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the Special Court was legally constituted and had jurisdiction to hear the case. 
  2. To what extent could freedom of speech and publication under the Constitution be restricted? 
  3. Whether Dr. K.I. Singh’s pamphlets and press statement amounted to creating hatred, malice or disaffection against the Government under Section 6 (2) of the Rajkaj (Offences and Punishment) Act. 
  4. Whether merely supporting or agreeing with Dr. K.I. Singh’s views was sufficient to establish criminal liability against Keshav Chandra Gautam.
  Different Courts Decisions: Special Court: The Special Court held that the actions of the defendants amounted to an offense against the state. It found Dr. K.I. Singh guilty and sentenced him to 2 years in prison and imposed a fine of Rs. 2,000. It also found co-defendant Keshav Chandra Gautam guilty and sentenced him to 1 year in prison along with a fine of Rs. 500. Supreme Court: The Supreme Court upheld the jurisdiction and constitutional validity of the Special Court, ruling that minor procedural errors in its formation did not invalidate its authority. Furthermore, the Court interpreted that the Constitution allows the state to enact laws restricting freedom of speech and expression if done for the public interest. Consequently, the Supreme Court affirmed that Dr. K.I. Singh’s pamphlets and statements constituted offenses of hatred and contempt against the government under the Rajkaj Act, and it upheld his conviction and sentence. Regarding Keshav Chandra Gautam, the Court held that his actions in distributing the pamphlets and giving speeches in support of Dr. Singh also established his criminal liability, thus upholding his conviction and sentence as well. Principles Established:
  1. A court’s decision will not be declared void due to minor procedural defects or clerical errors if there is no fundamental defect in its formation or the court’s jurisdiction.
  2. When interpreting phrases like “complaints made or to be made” under Section 3(1) of the Special Court Act, the law must be construed to cover prospective or future complaints, rather than being strictly restricted to existing ones.
  3. Fundamental rights, such as Article 11 (2) rights (freedom of speech and expression), are subject to restrictions imposed by law under Article 17, allowing the legislature to regulate these rights in the interest of the general public.
  4. The failure to strictly follow a procedural provision does not invalidate a case unless it causes actual harm or hindrance to the administration of justice

title: Interpretation of Law Case: Yagyamurti Banjade vs. Durga Das, NKP (6th Semester)
content:
Interpretation of Law Case: Parshuram Banjade, on behalf of Yagyamurti Banjade vs. Durga Das Shrestha, Bagmati Special Court, & Others, NKP 2027 B.S, Vol: 7, DN: 547. Case: Writ of Habeas Corpus Petitioner: Parshuram Banjade, on behalf of Yagyamurti Banjade Respondents: Durgadas Shrestha, Bagmati Special Court, & Others Decision Number: 547  

This case is related to statutory interpretation regarding legislative amendments, the scope of executive authority, principle of natural justice, the fundamental rights to legal representation and personal liberty.

Facts of the Case: On 18th Baisakh 2027 B.S., Yagyamurti Banjade and several other students were arrested at Naya Sadak, Kathmandu, by state security personnel dressed in civilian clothes. The arresting officers did not present an arrest warrant nor did they disclose the legal grounds for the arrest. Following this, the individuals were taken directly into custody and incarcerated at the Central Jail (Kendriya Karagar) of Kathmandu. The administration justified the detention by alleging that the students had formed an unauthorized organization, the “Nepal Students Union”, without government approval, which they claimed violated the National Guidance Act, 2019 B.S. However, a legislative amendment passed in 2024 B.S. had already explicitly removed the phrase “student union” from the statute’s prohibited list. Despite this legal reality, His Majesty’s Government published an official notification in the Nepal Gazette on 21st Baisakh 2027 B.S., delegating special judicial authority to Durga Das Shrestha, the Chairman of the Bagmati Special Court. On 29th Jestha 2027 B.S., the detainee was subjected to a late-evening, closed-door summary proceeding without public access or the opportunity to consult or be represented by a legal practitioner of his choice. Asserting that his brother was being subjected to illegal confinement without statutory backing and in clear violation of his constitutional rights, Parshuram Banjade filed a writ petition of Habeas Corpus directly before the Supreme Court of Nepal demanding Yagyamurti Banjade’s immediate release.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the removal of the phrase “student union” through a legislative amendment meant the activity was no longer prohibited under the National Direction Act.
  2. Whether an administrative officer exercising quasi-judicial powers is mandated to apply a judicial mind and adhere to the principles of natural justice.
  3. Whether conducting summary proceedings without informing the accused of their right to legal counsel violates the constitutional guarantee under Article 11(6) of the Constitution of Nepal.
  4. Whether the executive or a quasi-judicial body can curtail personal liberty without strict and literal compliance with both substantive and procedural laws.
  Decisions of the Courts: Bagmati Special Court: His Majesty’s Government delegated special quasi-judicial authority to Durga Das Shrestha, Chairman of the Bagmati Special Court, to act as the trial court for this matter. On 29th Jestha 2027 B.S., he conducted a hurried, closed-door interrogation of the detainees near Singha Durbar Putali Garden, without allowing them access to legal practitioners/lawyers. The Special Court ruled that forming the “Nepal Students Union” was an offense and issued a judicial order convicting the detainee and imposing a punishment of imprisonment and a fine, citing Section 53 of the Chapter on Punishment.  Supreme Court: The Division Bench of the Supreme Court quashed the order issued by Durga Das Shrestha of the Bagmati Special Court and issued a writ of Habeas Corpus, ordering the immediate release of the detainee. The Court held that because the legislature had deliberately omitted “student union” from the National Guidance Act, the detainee’s actions did not constitute a statutory offense. The Court further ruled that the trial conducted in closed doors without allowing legal representation was unconstitutional and void due to non-compliance with procedural and substantive law. Principles Established:
  1. When the legislature amends an Act and intentionally removes a specific word or phrase, courts must interpret that omission as a clear legislative intent to remove that subject matter entirely from the prohibition or scope of the statute.
  2. In a democratic system where personal freedom is paramount, if an act is not explicitly forbidden by law, it must be interpreted as legally permissible.
  3. Administrative officials tasked with making judicial determinations perform quasi-judicial functions and must maintain an impartial, judicial standpoint.
  4. The constitutional right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner is absolute; authorities cannot bypass this right by claiming the detainee did not proactively demand a lawyer.
  5. Any substantive or procedural law that empowers the state to deprive an individual of life or personal liberty must be interpreted strictly and adhered to letter by letter.

title: Interpretation of Law/ Property Law Case: Ratna Devi vs. Prem Man, NKP (6th Semester)
content:
Interpretation of Law/ Property Law Case: Prem Man Manandhar vs Ratna Devi Manandhar and Ganesh Man Manandhar, NKP 2042 B.S., Vol: 9, DN: 2493. Case: Partition of Property Plaintiff: Prem Man Manandhar Defendants: Ratna Devi Manandhar and Ganesh Man Manandhar Decision Number: 2493

This case is related to the partition of property. It is a foundational case for the Interpretation of Law, specifically establishing that laws should be interpreted reasonably (purposive approach) rather than using a hyper-literal approach that defeats legislative intent.

  Facts of the Case: The plaintiff, Prem Man Manandhar, filed a property partition lawsuit on 2035/2/18/4 B.S., claiming he had been living separately, with a separate kitchen since 2027/1/1 B.S. and demanding a one-third share of the family property under Sections 21, 22, and 23 of the Chapter on Partition in the Muluki Ain, 2020 B.S. His elder brother, Ganesh Man Manandhar, contested the claim, disputing the alleged separation and stating that their father, Ratna Man, had left government dues of Rs. 61,783.18 arising from a government contract. He argued that the matter concerning the government liability had not been settled and that the property could not therefore be partitioned, and also sought dismissal of the suit under Section 180 of the Chapter on Court Management. Furthermore, he referred to the family’s use of joint funds for their father’s cancer treatment in India from 2030 B.S. and disputed Ratnadevi's entitlement to a share on the ground that she had not reached the required age. Subsequently, on 2037/2/31/6 B.S., Ratnadevi stated that she was 38 years old and claimed her share in the family property. Another dispute concerned a house at Netpacho Tole purchased in 2028 B.S. and registered in the name of the plaintiff's wife, Krishna Devi Manandhar. Ganesh Man claimed that the house had been acquired using joint family funds and should therefore be included in the partition, while Krishna Devi maintained that it was her private property, having been purchased with a loan from her mother. A previous document relating to the registration of a mortgage over the property dated 2035/10/10/5 B.S. was also produced in connection with this dispute. Legal Issues:
  1. Whether unpaid government dues from a joint family be treated as a regular ‘debt’ that all family members must share. 
  2. Should the court read the law strictly word-for-word (hyper-literal interpretation), or should it interpret the law reasonably to match its true purpose?  
  3. Can a family divide its property while there are still unpaid government debts?  
  4. Should a house registered in a wife’s name be divided if it is claimed to be bought with joint family money? 
  Decisions of the Courts: Kathmandu District Court: The Kathmandu District Court held that Prem Man, Ganesh Man and Ratna Devi were all equally entitled to shares in the family property. Since Ratna Devi had attained the required age and was recognised as their sister, she was also entitled to a share. The court therefore treated the property as divisible into three equal shares, with Prem Man entitled to one-third. The issue of the government liability was left to be dealt with according to law if the liability was ultimately required to be recovered from the family. Madhyamanchal Regional Court: The court held that the government debt of Rs. 61,783.18 was a liability of the joint family. Therefore, all three co-sharers were responsible for the debt, and the plaintiff was required to bear one-third, amounting to Rs. 20,561.06. Regarding the house at Netpacho Tole registered in the plaintiff'’s wife’s name, the court held that it was necessary to determine whether the house had been purchased from joint family funds or from the wife’s private resources. It therefore left the parties to establish their respective rights over the property through appropriate proceedings. Supreme Court: The Supreme Court held that the government dues constituted a debt for partition. It rejected the argument that government dues were not “debt” merely because they were not an ordinary private debt, describing such an approach as a hyper-literal interpretation. The Court emphasised that legal interpretation must be reasonable and consistent with the principle of dividing both property and debt under the law. However, since the exact liability to be recovered from the family had not yet been finally determined, the Court held that the plaintiff could not be required to immediately pay one-third of the amount. The Regional Court’s order requiring Prem Man to pay Rs. 20,561.06 was therefore set aside, while the government dues remained recoverable from the responsible family members according to law. Principles Established:
  1. The interpretation of the law must be reasonable and not just strictly legal or hyper-literal. The court established that if a purely word for word interpretation completely contradicts the core principles of a statute, it should be rejected.  
  2. The government dues incurred while the family is in a joint state are legally categorized as a “debt”.
  3. Coparceners cannot use a hyper-literal reading of the law to avoid sharing liabilities. The foundational principle of the Chapter on Partition in the Muluki Ain requires the division of both “wealth and debt”. Therefore, government dues must be proportionately divided and shared among all coparceners alongside the family assets.
