title: Corporate Law Case: Re Smith & Fawcett Ltd. (6th Semester)
content:
Corporate Law Case: Re Smith & Fawcett Ltd. [1942] Ch. 304.  Case:  Directors’ Discretion and Good Faith. Plaintiff: Edwin Arthur Fawcett Defendant: Norman Smith and J. W. Feather Case Citation: [1942] Ch. 304.   

This case is related to Directors’ Discretion and Good Faith. 

Facts of the Case: Smith and Fawcett Ltd was a private company. Joseph Fawcett and Norman Smith were its two directors and shareholders, each holding 4,001 ordinary shares. Fawcett died, and his shares were to pass to his son, Edwin Fawcett. The executors of Fawcett’s estate asked the company to register the transfer of all 4,001 shares in Edwin’s name. The company’s articles gave the directors an “absolute and uncontrolled discretion” to refuse registration of a share transfer. Relying on this power, Smith refused to register all the shares in Edwin’s name. He offered to register 2,001 shares and to buy the remaining 2,000 shares himself. Edwin challenged the refusal and asked the court to rectify the company’s register by registering him as the holder of all 4,001 shares. He claimed that Smith had used the directors’ power for his own benefit and to maintain control of the company.   Legal Issues:
  1. What was the extent of the directors’ power to refuse registration of a share transfer?
  2. Whether the directors had to exercise that power honestly and in the interests of the company.
  3. Whether the directors had used their power for a personal or collateral purpose.
  4. Whether the court could interfere with the directors’ decision.
Decision of the Court: The Chancery Division dismissed the application. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision. The Court of Appeal held that the wording of the articles gave the directors a very wide discretion to refuse registration of share transfers. However, this discretion was not completely unrestricted. As a fiduciary power, it had to be exercised bona fide, meaning honestly and in what the directors themselves considered to be the interests of the company. It could not be used for a collateral or improper purpose. The court also held that the question was not whether the court itself considered the decision to be in the company’s best interests. The relevant question was whether the directors had honestly exercised their discretion in what they believed to be the company’s interests. On the evidence, the court found no sufficient proof that Smith had acted in bad faith or for a collateral purpose. The directors had bona fide considered the interests of the company and decided that registering the entire transfer would be undesirable. Therefore, the refusal to register all 4,001 shares was valid, and the court refused to interfere with the directors’ decision.   Principles Established:
  1. Directors must exercise powers given by the company’s articles bona fide in the interests of the company.
  2. A wide or “absolute” discretion given to directors is not a licence to act for an improper purpose.
  3. Directors must not use their powers for a collateral or personal purpose.
  4. The court generally will not interfere with a directors’ decision when the power has been exercised honestly and within its proper purpose.
  5. The directors’ decision is judged by what they honestly considered to be in the company’s interests, not simply by what the court itself considers best.
rationale: Classification resolved to CASE_LAW, but subject cannot be determined safely.

title: Election Law Case: Communist Party of Nepal v. Election Commission, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Election Law Case: Communist Party of Nepal v. Election Commission, N.K.P.2051, Vol. 36, DN: 4950 Case: Certiorari with Mandamus Petitioner: Nepal Communist Party  , through Prabhunarayan Chaudhary Respondents: Chief Election Commissioner, Election Commission and Others Decision Number: 4950

This case is about the registration and electoral recognition of a political party.

  Facts of the Case: The Nepal Communist Party, established on 15 September 1949, through its organizer Prabhunarayan Chaudhary, wanted to participate in the House of Representatives and local elections under its own political identity and election symbol. For this purpose, the party submitted an application to the Election Commission on 2048/11/15 B.S. seeking official recognition and registration for electoral purposes. However, by a letter dated 2048/12/13 B.S., the Election Commission refused to process the application. The Commission stated that the period for party registration had already expired and that the House of Representatives election had already been completed. It further relied on Article 113(2)(d) of the Constitution of Nepal, 2047, which required a political party to obtain at least 3% of the total votes cast in the previous House of Representatives election to receive electoral recognition and an election symbol. The Nepal Communist Party challenged this decision before the Supreme Court through a writ petition. The party argued that it was a new political party, and therefore it was impossible for it to have obtained 3% of the votes in an election that had taken place before the party was formed. It further argued that denying registration on this ground would prevent new parties from participating in elections and would weaken the constitutional principle of multiparty democracy guaranteed by the Constitution. Therefore, the party requested the Court to quash the Election Commission's decision and direct it to recognize the party and provide it with an election symbol according to law.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the writ petition had become meaningless because the local election had already ended.
  2. Whether a political party has the right to participate in elections as a political party even if it had not yet obtained 3% of votes in a previous election.
  3. Whether a newly formed political party could be denied registration because it had not obtained 3% votes in an election held before it was formed.
  4. Whether the Election Commission's decision and the relevant provision of the Local Bodies Election Procedure Act, 2048 were inconsistent with the Constitution.
  5. Whether the political party was entitled to its own election symbol.
  Decision of the Court: Supreme Court-Special Bench: The Supreme Court held that a new political party could not be denied registration on the ground that it had failed to obtain 3% of the votes in a previous election held before the party existed. The Court therefore quashed the Election Commission's decision and directed it to recognize the party and allow it to participate in elections according to law.  Principle Established: A new political party cannot be denied registration merely because it did not obtain 3% of votes in a previous election held before the party was formed. The 3% requirement must be understood in a manner consistent with the constitutional guarantee of multiparty democracy and the freedom to establish political parties.  Relevancy of the Case: This case is important in Constitutional Law and Election Law because it protects the right to form and operate political parties and strengthens Nepal's multiparty democratic system. It also explains how constitutional rights should be interpreted so that they are practical rather than impossible to exercise. Most importantly, the case prevents a newly formed political party from being denied registration on the basis of a 3% vote requirement from an election that took place before the party existed. It is also relevant to writ jurisdiction, particularly  Certiorari and Mandamus.
rationale: Title clearly represents distinct academic subject (Election Law) absent from Prisma.

title: Election  Law Case: Mangol National Organisation  v. Election Commission, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Election Law Case: Mangol National Organisation  v. Election Commission, NKP: 2052, Volume: 3, No.1, P.19, DN: 5030 Case: Mandamus, Certiorari and other appropriate orders Petitioner: Gopal Gurung, President of Mangol National Organisation Respondents: Election Commission and Others Decision Number: 5030  

This case concerned the registration of the Mongol National Organisation as a political party for election purposes.

  Facts of the Case: Gopal Gurung, President of the Mongol National Organisation, applied to the Election Commission on 2047/10/08 to register his organisation as a political party for election purposes. Along with the application, he submitted the organisation’s constitution and manifesto. The Election Commission asked Gurung to clarify certain provisions of the organisation’s constitution. After receiving his clarification, the Commission decided on 2047/11/03 not to register the Mongol National Organisation. Gurung was informed about the decision on 2047/11/05. The Election Commission stated that the organisation’s name, objectives and flag were inconsistent with Article 113(3) of the Constitution of 2047. It also stated that the organisation could not be registered under Section 17(2) of the House of Representatives Election Act, 2047. According to the Commission, some of the organisation’s objectives appeared to distinguish between Nepalese citizens based on their ancestry. The Commission considered that such objectives could create division among Nepalese citizens. Gopal Gurung challenged the Election Commission’s decision before the Supreme Court. He requested the Court to quash the Commission’s decision and order the Commission to register the Mongol National Organisation as a political party. He also requested an interim order to stop the upcoming election until the Supreme Court finally decided the writ petition. Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the Election Commission's decision not to register the Mongol National Organisation was constitutional and lawful.
  2. Whether refusal to register the organisation violated the constitutional freedom to form political organisations and parties.
  3. Whether a political organisation based on religion, caste, race, language or similar communal considerations could be registered for election purposes.
  4. Whether the name, objectives and flag of the Mongol National Organisation were contrary to Article 113(3) of the Constitution of Nepal, 2047.
  5. Whether the applicant's constitutional or legal rights had been violated by the Election Commission's refusal to register the organisation.
Decision of the Court: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petition. It held that although citizens have the constitutional freedom to form political organisations or parties, such freedom is not absolute. A political party seeking registration must comply with the constitutional and legal requirements. Since the Mongol National Organisation's objectives, name and flag were found to have a communal and divisive character and were inconsistent with Article 113(3) of the Constitution of Nepal, 2047, the Election Commission was justified in refusing its registration. Therefore, the refusal to register the organisation did not violate the applicant's constitutional or legal rights, and the writ petition was dismissed.  Principle Established: The right to form a political party is subject to constitutional limitations. A political organisation whose membership, name, objectives, symbol or flag is discriminatory, communal or likely to promote division among citizens cannot claim registration for election purposes, and the Election Commission may lawfully refuse its registration.

title: Election Law Case:  Peshal Dahal & Others v. Parliament Secretariat , NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Election Law Case: Peshal Dahal & Others v. Parliament Secretariat,  NKP 2056, Vol. 41, No. 1, P.6, DN: 6648 Case: Certiorari Petitioner: Dr. Peshal Dahal and 2 Others Respondents: Parliament Secretariat and 3 Others Decision Number: 6648  

This case is about the constitutional validity of Section 7(c) of the Voter List Act, 2052, concerning the voter-registration rights of persons residing in places such as employee residences and hostels.

Facts of the Case: Dr. Peshal Dahal and two other petitioners were Nepali citizens who were living in Kathmandu for different purposes. Dr. Peshal Dahal had been teaching at Tribhuvan University, Kirtipur, since 2038 and had been residing in the professor's residential quarters since 2047. Another petitioner, Sundar Bahadur Tumbahamphe, was working at Teaching Hospital, Maharajgunj, and was living in the hospital's residential quarters. The third petitioner, Ved Prakash Jaisi Bhattarai, was studying at Ascol Campus and was residing in the campus hostel. The petitioners challenged Section 7(c) of the Voter List Act, 2052, which provided that persons residing in employee residential quarters, military or police barracks, industrial establishments' housing, hospitals, schools, colleges, hostels, orphanages, old-age homes, prisons and similar places would not be considered permanently residing in that electoral area. The petitioners argued that this provision was inconsistent with the constitutional guarantee of adult suffrage and violated their rights under Articles 3, 11, 12 and 45 of the Constitution of Nepal, 2047. They also argued that persons living in such residences could be unable to register as voters either in their permanent residence or in their current place of residence. They therefore requested the Supreme Court to declare Section 7(c) unconstitutional and invalid and to issue appropriate writs, including certiorari and mandamus. The Election Commission defended the provision, arguing that its purpose was to ensure that a person could vote in only one electoral constituency and to prevent duplicate voter registration. According to the Commission, a person temporarily living in an employee residence, hostel or similar place continued to have permanent residence in their original electoral constituency and could register there. Legal Issues:
  1. Whether Section 7(c) of the Voter List Act, 2052 was consistent with the Constitution of Nepal, 2047.
  2. Whether Section 7(c) violated the petitioners' constitutional right to vote under Article 45(6).
  3. Whether the provision violated the right to equality under Article 11 of the Constitution.
  4. Whether the provision was inconsistent with the constitutional freedom of movement and residence and the freedom to choose a profession, occupation, trade or business under Article 12(2)(d) and (e).
  5. Whether treating persons residing in employee quarters, hospitals, hostels and similar places as not permanently residing there created an unconstitutional restriction on voting rights.    
  Decision of the Court: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petition, holding that Section 7(c) of the Voter List Act, 2052 was not inconsistent with the Constitution. The Court held that a person living temporarily in places such as employee quarters or hostels could still vote in their permanent electoral constituency. Therefore, practical inconvenience did not amount to denial of the right to vote.  Principle Established: The right to vote in one electoral constituency is subject to the procedure established by law. Practical inconvenience in voting does not amount to deprivation of the constitutional right to vote.

title: Election Law Case: Mihir Kumar Thakur v. Election Commission , NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Election Law Case: Mihir Kumar Thakur v. Election Commission , NKP 2062, Vol. 47, No. 5, P.593, DN: 7541 Case: Mandamus Petitioner: Advocate Mihir Kumar Thakur and Others Respondents: Election Commission and Others Decision Number: 7541

This case concerns transparency in election financing and the requirement of a clean and fair election.

Facts of the Case: The petitioner, Janahit Sanrakshan Manch, through Advocate Mihir Kumar Thakur, filed a writ petition concerning the general election scheduled for 2059/07/27. The petitioner argued that political parties and candidates could spend large amounts of money and collect donations from unknown sources, which could influence voters and affect the free, fair and clean election process. The petitioner therefore sought an order requiring political parties to disclose their election income, sources of funds and election expenditure, and to have such accounts properly audited and submitted to the Election Commission. The petitioner relied, among other things, on the right to information under Article 16 of the Constitution of Nepal, 2047, and referred to the duties and powers of the Election Commission under existing election laws. The petitioner also requested that election laws be amended to regulate matters such as political donations, disclosure of sources of election funds, auditing of political party accounts, and limits on election expenditure. During the case, the general election scheduled for 2059/07/27 was postponed. Further, the Political Parties Act, 2058 came into force on 2059/05/27 and introduced provisions requiring registered political parties to maintain accounts, have them audited, submit annual financial reports to the Election Commission, and make those reports public. However, the Election Commission informed the Court that the required annual reports had not yet been submitted, and consequently the Commission had not published the required reports either. Legal Issues: 1. Whether political parties and candidates' election income and expenditure should be made publicly transparent to ensure a clean and fair election. 2. Whether the existing legal provisions requiring political parties to disclose and audit their financial information were being effectively implemented. 3. Whether the Election Commission should take necessary measures to implement existing law and address matters not adequately regulated by law. Decision of the Court: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court held that excessive election spending and undisclosed political funding can affect the fairness of elections. Since the election scheduled for 2059/07/27 had already been postponed, no order was needed for that election. However, the Court found that financial transparency in elections was still important and directed the Election Commission to effectively implement the existing financial-disclosure provisions and make necessary legal arrangements for matters not covered by law. Principle Established: Transparency in the election finances of political parties and candidates is essential for ensuring clean and fair elections, as undisclosed funding and excessive expenditure can influence voters and distort the electoral process. Existing legal provisions on financial disclosure must be effectively implemented, and additional legal measures should be introduced where existing laws are insufficient.

title: Election Law Case: Advocate Kamlesh Dwivedi v. Prime Minister & Cabinet Secretariat, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Election Law Case: Advocate Kamlesh Dwivedi v. Prime Minister & Cabinet Secretariat, NKP 2064, Vol. 49, No. 7, P. 827, DN: 7866 Case: Certiorari and related reliefs ( Constitutional) Petitioner: Advocate Kamlesh Dwivedi and et al. Respondents: Government authorities, Legislature-Parliament and Others Decision Number: 7866

This case concerns the constitutional validity of Section 19(g) of the Constituent Assembly Member Election Act, 2064, which disqualified certain persons from contesting the Constituent Assembly election based on an Inquiry Commission report.

Facts of the Case: After the political changes of 2062/63, the Government formed a High-Level Inquiry Commission under the Inquiry Commission Act, 2026, headed by former Supreme Court Justice Krishna Jung Rayamajhi, to investigate acts committed during the suppression of the People's Movement and to recommend legal action against persons found responsible. Later, the Constituent Assembly Member Election Act, 2064 was enacted. Section 19(g) provided that a person holding a political appointment who was shown guilty in the Inquiry Commission's report for matters such as loss of life or property, misuse of power or position, human rights violations, or misuse of the national treasury would be considered ineligible to become a candidate in the Constituent Assembly election. Several political figures who intended to contest the Constituent Assembly election challenged this provision before the Supreme Court. They argued that an Inquiry Commission only investigates and makes recommendations; it does not have the authority to determine criminal guilt or impose punishment. They further argued that making a person ineligible for election merely because the Commission's report showed that person as guilty, without a judicial decision, violated the constitutional right to equality, freedom, justice and due process, including the principle that a person should not be treated as guilty until guilt is established through legal proceedings. The petitioners therefore asked the Supreme Court to declare Section 19(g) unconstitutional and void and to prevent the authorities from using that provision to deny them the right to participate in the Constituent Assembly election. Legal Issues: 1. Whether Section 19(छ) of the Constituent Assembly Member Election Act, 2064 was consistent with the Interim Constitution of Nepal, 2063. 2. Whether an Inquiry Commission report could, by itself, be used to declare a person ineligible to contest an election without a judicial decision. 3. Whether the provision violated the constitutional rights to freedom, equality and justice and the principle of separation of powers. Decision of the Court: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court held that an Inquiry Commission is not a judicial body. It cannot declare a person legally guilty. The Court held that Section 19(g) was unconstitutional. It disqualified a person from contesting an election solely on the basis of an Inquiry Commission report, without a judicial decision. This violated the constitutional rights to freedom, equality and justice. Therefore, the Court declared Section 19(g) of the Constituent Assembly Member Election Act, 2064 unconstitutional and void under Article 107(1) of the Interim Constitution, 2063. Principle Established: An Inquiry Commission is a fact-finding and recommending body, not a court. Its report cannot by itself be treated as a judicial finding of guilt or used to impose a legal disability such as election disqualification. Any determination of guilt carrying legal consequences must be made through a proper judicial process.

title: Fiscal Law Case: Pitambar Prasad Acharya & Others vs. Ministry of Finance & Others, NKP (7th Semester, Old & New Syllabus)
content:
Fiscal Law Case: Pitambar Prasad Acharya & Others vs. Ministry of Finance & Others, Nepal Kanoon Patrika (NKP), DN: 9143, No. 4, P. 422.   Case: Certiorari/Mandamus Plaintiff/Applicant: Pitambar Prasad Acharya on behalf of Development Project Service Centre (DEPROSC Nepal) Defendant/Respondent: Government of Nepal, Ministry of Finance, Department of Inland Revenue and others Decision Number: 9143  

This case is related to income tax law.

  Facts of the Case: DEPROSC Nepal was registered on 2050/06/10 BS under the Associations Registration Act, 2034 and it works on poverty alleviation in line with government policy. It has worked in 54 of Nepal’s 75 districts and has built irrigation, drinking water, health post, school, rural road, suspension bridge, community building and micro-hydro projects 7,647 in total. The Inland Revenue Office gave it a tax exemption certificate on 2061/05/01 BS and it filed annual financial statements every year. With Nepal Rastra Bank’s permission it ran a microfinance programme for poor rural women. On 2069/03/24 BS the tax office asked for documents and by letters of 2069/10/11 and 2069/10/14 it treated the following as taxable net income:
  • Rs 28,38,816.65 for FY 2056/57
  • Rs 29,59,924.45 for FY 2057/58
  • Rs 21,66,09,029.43 in total for FY 2058/59 to 2067/68
The office relied on the organization’s income from bank loan investments, microfinance interest, consultancy, bank deposit interest and others. It also cited grants taken without government approval and profits from competitively bid projects. The organization went straight to the Supreme Court instead of using the review and appeal route in the tax law. Plaintiff’s Claim: The tax exempt status was recognized by the tax office itself and the certificate was never cancelled nor declared inactive. Section 42(1)(Cha) of the then Income Tax Act 2031 and Section 2(Dha)(1)(Ka) of the existing Income Tax Act 2058 exempt non profit public benefit organizations. It had not breached the conditions of its certificate nor acted outside its objectives. Defendant’s arguments: Under Section 115 of the Income Tax Act 2058 the organization could seek administrative review before the Department of Inland Revenue and then appeal to the Revenue Tribunal but skipped this so the writ should be dismissed.   Legal Issues:
  1. Can writ jurisdiction be invoked against a tax office’s decision when alternative remedies exist?
  2. Is the petitioner a service-oriented, tax-exempt organization under Section 42(1)(Cha) of the Income Tax Act 2031 and Section 2(Dha)(1)(Ka) of the Income Tax Act 2058?
  3. Can a service oriented non-profit organization carry out financial transactions and is income from them taxable?
  4. Should the writ order requested be issued?
  Different Courts Decision: Supreme Court: The Court held that a disputed legal question in a tax authority’s decision cannot be said to be beyond writ jurisdiction. The authority is competent to decide which income is taxable but if that is contrary to law a writ can address that. It accepted that DEPROSC Nepal is a genuine service oriented non profit organization. The Court held that being non profit does not exempt all income. Financial transactions are not purely service as they are also profit-oriented business and net profit from such business cannot be tax free. The Court further held that tax exemption has its own limits and a certificate does not make all income tax free and it is wrong to argue that business income cannot be taxed. The tax office ignored Sections 24 and 31 of the Financial Intermediary Institutions Act 2055 under which the government may grant full or partial income tax exemption on microfinance income. No such exemption decision had been made. The tax office did not analyse which income was taxable and which was exempt as it taxed the entire amount including amounts that should not have been taxed. The Court issued certiorari quashing the decision of 2069/10/08 and the assessment orders and letters of 2069/10/11 and 2069/10/11 and 2069/10/14 and also issued mandamus directing the respondents to evaluate the evidence and decide the organization’s tax liability afresh within 3 months. The judgment quashed the orders on the ground of failure to separate taxable and exempt income.   Principle Established:
  1. An assessment that lumps all income of a non profit organization without following the legal steps to separate taxable and exempt income is not lawful and can be quashed.
  2. Tax authorities are competent to decide what is taxable and what is not but if they act contrary to law or a legal question is in dispute that question can be resolved through writ jurisdiction.
  3. Being non-profit does not exempt all income and a non profit organization that carries on commercial or financial business cannot claim exemption on all of that income.
  4. Tax exemption has its own limits. A tax exemption certificate does not make an organization tax free on pure business income.
  Relevancy of the Case: This case is a leading authority on the tax treatment of NGOs, cooperatives and microfinance institutions in Nepal. It balances two things: exemption for genuine non-profit work and taxation of business and financial income.

content:
Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sapana Pradhan Malla vs. Government of Nepal & Others, NKP (7th Semester) Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sapana Pradhan Malla vs. Government of Nepal & Others, (NKP) (2065), No. 8, P. 917, DN: 8031 Case: certiorari  Plaintiff: Sapana Pradhan Malla et.al. Defendant: Government of Nepal, Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers Decision Number: 8031   The case is relating to equality in parental property and inheritance rights between married and unmarried daughters under the Muluki Ain, 2020.    Facts: The Muluki Ain, 2020 contained different rules for a daughter’s right to receive property from her parental family depending on whether she was married or unmarried. Section 1(a) of the Partition Chapter provided that an unmarried daughter could receive a share of her parental property. However, once she got married, she was no longer entitled to receive a share from her parents under that provision. Thus, marriage could result in the loss of her right to claim a share in parental property. Section 2 of the Inheritance Chapter also placed a married daughter lower in the order of inheritance. A husband, wife, son and unmarried daughter were given priority as heirs. A married daughter could inherit from her parents only when the heirs having priority under the law were absent. The law also limited the circumstances in which a daughter's child could inherit property from the maternal grandparents. In certain situations, the right depended on the daughter's marital status.   Plaintiff's Claims: The petitioners argued that the law discriminated between sons and daughters and also between married and unmarried daughters. They claimed that a woman should not lose or have her parental property rights restricted merely because she married. They argued that such discrimination violated the constitutional right to equality and equal property rights and weakened women's economic independence. Defendants' Arguments: The defendants argued that the provisions were not discriminatory because an unmarried daughter could receive property from her parents, while a married woman could receive property from her husband's family. They argued that allowing a married daughter to inherit from both families could give her an additional benefit compared with other heirs. They also argued that inheritance should follow the legal order of heirs and that changing these rules was a matter for the legislature. Legal Issues:
  1. Whether denying a married daughter a share in parental property violated the constitutional right to equality.
  2. Whether giving an unmarried daughter priority over a married daughter in inheritance was discriminatory.
  3. Whether the provisions violated the equal property rights of sons and daughters.
  4. Whether the Supreme Court could direct the legislature to replace the challenged provisions.
Different Court Decisions: Supreme Court: The Special Bench dismissed the writ petition. The Court held that an unmarried daughter was not completely excluded from receiving property from her parents. It also considered that, after marriage, a woman obtained property rights in her husband's family under the law then in force. On this basis, the Court did not find the different treatment of married and unmarried daughters to be unconstitutional discrimination. The Court further reasoned that inheritance was not determined only by sex. The law also considered the closeness of the legal relationship with the deceased and the responsibility to care for the deceased. Therefore, the different position given to a married daughter was treated as a legal classification rather than discrimination based solely on gender. The Court upheld the challenged provisions and dismissed the writ petition.   Principles Established:
  1. Equality does not always require identical treatment.
  2. Different treatment is valid when it is based on a reasonable legal classification.
  3. A legal classification must not unfairly deny constitutional rights.
  4. Under the law then in force, marriage could create separate property rights through the husband.
  5. Inheritance could be based on the closeness of the legal relationship and responsibility towards the deceased.
  6. Property laws should be developed to strengthen the position of disadvantaged groups and ensure effective enjoyment of their rights.
rationale: Classification resolved to CASE_LAW, but subject cannot be determined safely.

title: Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sapana Pradhan Malla vs. Government of Nepal & Others, NKP (7th Semester)
content:
Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sapana Pradhan Malla vs. Government of Nepal & Others, (NKP) (2065), No. 8, P. 917, DN: 7997 Case: Certiorari and Mandamus Plaintiff: Sapana Pradhan Malla Defendant: Government of Nepal et.al. Decision Number: 7997

This case is relating to gender discrimination, polygamy, domestic violence, and equality of spouses under marriage law.

Facts of the Case: Sapana Pradhan Malla and other lawyers connected with the Forum for Women, Law and Development filed a public-interest petition before the Supreme Court of Nepal. They challenged Sections 9 and 9A of the Marriage Chapter of the Muluki Ain. Section 9 allowed a husband to marry another woman while his wife was still alive in certain situations. These situations included when the wife had an incurable sexually transmitted disease, was incurably mentally ill, could not have children because of her own condition, could not walk, was blind in both eyes, or had taken her share of the property and lived separately. Section 9A required the wife’s consent before the husband could marry again in some of these situations. However, her consent was not required when she was incurably mentally ill or when she had taken her share of the property and lived separately. The petitioners argued that these provisions treated the husband and wife unequally. They placed the burden on the woman because of her illness, disability, inability to have children, or decision to live separately after taking her share of property. The petitioners also argued that the provisions could encourage domestic violence. A husband might pressure, threaten, or harm his wife to obtain her consent for another marriage. The provisions could also make a woman choose between her property rights and her marital relationship. The challenge was made under the Interim Constitution of Nepal, 2007. The petitioners also relied on the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and other international human-rights instruments. Plaintiff's Claims: The petitioners argued that Sections 9 and 9A discriminated against women and violated their rights to equality, dignity, liberty, family life, property, and freedom from violence. They argued that a woman's illness or disability should not become a legal ground for her husband to marry another woman. They also argued that requiring the wife’s consent could expose her to pressure, threats, or domestic violence. The petitioners asked the Court to strike down the discriminatory provisions and direct the Government to make laws consistent with gender equality. Defendants' Arguments: The Government argued that Section 9 was intended to regulate and discourage polygamy by allowing it only in limited situations. It argued that Section 9A protected women by requiring their consent in most cases. It also stated that women could seek legal protection if force or violence was used. The Government further argued that striking down the provisions completely could create a legal gap. It stated that legal reform was already being considered. Legal Questions:
  1. Whether Sections 9 and 9A discriminated against women.
  2. Whether a husband could marry another woman because of his wife’s illness, disability, infertility, or separate residence.
  3. Whether the consent requirement could expose women to pressure or domestic violence.
  4. Whether the provisions were consistent with the Interim Constitution and CEDAW.
  Different Court Decisions: Supreme Court Decision: The Supreme Court examined the disputed provisions in light of gender equality, women’s dignity, freedom from violence, and Nepal’s international obligations under CEDAW. The Court observed that most of the grounds in Section 9 related to the wife’s health or disability. A wife suffering from serious illness, mental illness, blindness, or physical disability usually needed greater care and support from her husband. Her condition should not automatically become an opportunity for the husband to marry another woman. The Court also noted that Section 9A did not require the wife’s consent when she was incurably mentally ill or when she had taken her share of property and lived separately. These exceptions could expose vulnerable women to further harm. The Court held that the possibility of pressure, threats, and domestic violence had to be taken seriously. A legal provision should not be used in a way that allows a husband to obtain consent through fear or force. The Court did not immediately declare all of Sections 9 and 9A void. It considered that striking down the entire provisions could create a legal gap. The Court also considered the Government’s stated commitment to reform gender-discriminatory laws. Instead, the Court used its constitutional power to issue a directive order. It ordered the Government to amend Sections 9 and 9A so that they would be consistent with the Interim Constitution and CEDAW. The amended law had to remove discrimination between husbands and wives and prevent women from experiencing further violence or unequal treatment. Principles Established:
  1. Marriage laws must provide equal treatment to men and women.
  2. A woman’s illness, disability, or infertility cannot by itself justify discriminatory treatment.
  3. Consent must be free and voluntary.
  4. Laws should not expose women to pressure, threats, or domestic violence.
  5. The State must remove discriminatory laws and practices against women.
  6. CEDAW must be reflected in Nepal’s domestic laws and legal practice.
  7. Equality applies to marriage, family life, property, and personal dignity.

title: Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Laxmi Dhikta & Others vs. Government of Nepal, NKP (7th semester)
content:
Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Laxmi Dhikta & Others vs. Government of Nepal, NKP (2067), P. 1551, DN: 8464 Case: Mandamus Plaintiff: Laxmi Dhikta Defendant: Government of Nepal, Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers Decision Number: 8464  

The case is relating to the right to safe and accessible abortion, reproductive rights, and the State’s duty to provide legal abortion services.

  Facts: Lakshmi Devi Dhikta, a woman from Ajayameru, Dadeldhura, had already given birth to five children. She later became pregnant again but did not want to continue the pregnancy. At that time, Nepalese law permitted abortion in certain circumstances and required the service to be provided through approved health workers and institutions. Lakshmi and her husband therefore went to Dadeldhura Hospital to obtain an abortion. The hospital required her to pay Rs. 1,130 for the service. Lakshmi was unable to pay the amount because of her financial condition. As a result, she could not obtain the abortion and was compelled to continue the pregnancy and give birth to another child. The case was brought before the Supreme Court as a public-interest petition concerning access to abortion services. The petition also raised concerns about the practical availability of abortion services in Nepal. At the time, safe abortion services were not equally available in all districts, particularly in rural areas. Women could also face difficulties in obtaining information about legal abortion, finding trained service providers, and paying the required fees. The petition further concerned the need for proper regulation of abortion services, including service fees, confidentiality of women seeking abortion, availability of trained health workers and health facilities, and public awareness about the legal availability of abortion. Plaintiff's Claims: The petitioners claimed that legalising abortion was not sufficient if women could not actually access safe and affordable services. They argued that the State had a duty to make abortion services accessible, affordable, confidential and properly regulated, particularly for poor and rural women. Lakshmi also sought compensation for the harm she suffered after being unable to obtain the abortion. Defendants' Arguments: The Government argued that Nepalese law had already legalised abortion in specified circumstances and that procedures had been established for providing safe abortion services. It stated that trained health workers and approved institutions were providing the service and that free services were available to poor women in appropriate cases. The Government also maintained that patient confidentiality was protected and that making or changing laws was primarily the responsibility of the legislature. Legal Issues:
  1. Whether access to safe abortion is part of women's reproductive rights.
  2. Whether the State has a duty to make legally permitted abortion services accessible and affordable.
  3. Whether failure to provide affordable abortion services violates women's constitutional rights.
  4. Whether the existing legal and institutional framework was sufficient to protect women's reproductive rights.
Different Court Decisions: Supreme Court: A Joint Bench of the Supreme Court, comprising Justices Kalyan Shrestha and Rajendra Prasad Koirala, allowed the petition in important respects. The Court recognised reproductive rights as including a woman's right to make decisions concerning whether and when to have children. This included the right to decide not to continue an unwanted pregnancy. The Court therefore treated abortion not merely as a matter of criminal law but also as a matter connected with women's reproductive rights and health. The Court held that merely recognising abortion as a legal right was not sufficient. Women had to be able to actually access the service. The State therefore had a responsibility to ensure that legal abortion services were safe, affordable, accessible and of proper quality. The Court directed the authorities to improve the availability of abortion services, establish appropriate and consistent fees, protect the confidentiality of women seeking abortion, and conduct public-awareness programmes about the service. The Court also directed the Government to take necessary steps towards developing a separate and adequate legal framework concerning abortion. However, the Court did not award compensation to Lakshmi. It found that there was insufficient objective evidence to determine the amount of compensation for the loss claimed. Principles Established:
  1. Reproductive rights include the right to decide whether and when to have children.
  2. Reproductive choice includes the right not to continue an unwanted pregnancy.
  3. A legally recognised right must be practically accessible to those entitled to exercise it.
  4. The State has a duty to provide accessible, affordable and safe abortion services.
  5. Poverty should not prevent a woman from accessing a legally available health service.
  6. Women seeking abortion are entitled to protection of their privacy and confidentiality.
  7. Abortion is not only a criminal-law issue but also a matter of reproductive health and women's rights.
  8. The State has a duty to provide proper information, trained health workers and adequate health facilities for legal abortion services.
  9. Where compensation is claimed, the loss must be supported by sufficient evidence to determine the amount.

title: Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sabina Damai vs. Government of Nepal & Others, NKP (7th Semester)
content:
Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sabina Damai vs. Government of Nepal & Others, NKP (2068), Р. 247, DN: 8557

Case: Mandamus Plaintiff: Sabina Damai et.al. Defendant: Government of Nepal, Office of the PM and Council of Ministers Decision Number: 8557

The case is relating to citizenship through a Nepali mother, equality in citizenship rights, and whether an unknown father can prevent a person from obtaining citizenship.

Facts: Sabina Damai was an 18 year old woman from Dolakha. Her mother, Gangamaya Damai, was a Nepali citizen by descent. Sabina’s father was unknown, and neither Sabina nor her mother knew his identity or address. Sabina sought Nepali citizenship through her mother. She completed the required procedure, submitted the necessary documents to the concerned local authority, and appeared for verification. She then applied to the District Administration Office, Dolakha, for a citizenship certificate based on her mother’s Nepali citizenship. The Chief District Officer refused to issue her the citizenship certificate. The officer stated that Sabina’s father had not been identified and that his address was unknown. Her application was returned orally on that ground. The absence of a citizenship certificate created difficulties for Sabina in proving her legal identity and accessing rights and services connected with citizenship, including employment, property and political rights. The case was also brought as a public-interest petition because similar difficulties were reportedly faced by other children of Nepali mothers. The dispute therefore concerned not only Sabina’s individual application but also the practice of requiring information about a father when a person sought citizenship through a Nepali mother. The petitioners relied on the constitutional provisions on citizenship and equality, the Nepal Citizenship Act, 2006, the Citizenship Rules, 2006, and relevant international human-rights instruments. Plaintiff's Claims: The petitioners claimed that Sabina was entitled to citizenship through her Nepali mother and that the identity or address of her father was not a legal requirement. They argued that refusing her citizenship violated her rights to citizenship, identity and equality and discriminated against children seeking citizenship through their mothers. Defendants' Arguments: The respondents argued that citizenship could be issued only after the required legal procedure and verification had been completed. The District Administration Office maintained that Sabina’s father's details had not been established and that she had not accepted a certificate describing her parental information in the manner permitted by law. They also argued that other legal remedies were available and sought dismissal of the petition. Legal Issues:
  1. Whether a person born in Nepal to a Nepali mother could obtain citizenship through the mother's name.
  2. Whether the identity or address of the father was necessary for issuing citizenship through the mother.
  3. Whether refusing citizenship because the father was unknown violated the right to equality and identity.
  4. Whether the Court could issue directions to prevent similar denial of citizenship to others.
  Different Court Decisions: Administrative Decision: The Chief District Officer of Dolakha refused to issue Sabina's citizenship certificate because her father's identity and address were unknown. Supreme Court: The Supreme Court allowed the petition and held that the constitutional expression “father or mother” could not be interpreted as requiring information about both parents. Where the Constitution recognised either parent, the citizenship process could not make the father's identity an additional requirement when the claim was based on a Nepali mother. The Court held that the authorities had wrongly refused Sabina's application merely because her father was unknown. The absence of information about her father could not, by itself, deprive her of the right to obtain citizenship through her Nepali mother. The Court also considered the discriminatory effect of a practice that effectively gave greater importance to the father than the mother in citizenship matters. It emphasised that constitutional rights could not be restricted by patriarchal social practices or administrative assumptions. The Court ordered the District Administration Office to issue Sabina's citizenship certificate through her mother's name. It also directed the Home Ministry to circulate appropriate instructions to Chief District Officers so that children born in Nepal to Nepali mothers would not face the same difficulty merely because their fathers were unknown. The Court further directed the Government to take measures to address discriminatory practices and raise public awareness regarding women's equal citizenship rights. Principles Established:
  1. Citizenship may be obtained through a Nepali father or mother where the law provides for either parent.
  2. “Father or mother” cannot be interpreted as requiring proof of both parents.
  3. An unknown father cannot, by itself, be a reason to deny citizenship through a Nepali mother.
  4. Citizenship is closely connected with legal identity and the exercise of other rights.
  5. Citizenship authorities must apply the law without gender discrimination.
  6. Patriarchal practices cannot override constitutional rights.

title: Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Meera Dhungana vs. Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs & Others, NKP (7th Semester)
content:
Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Meera Dhungana vs. Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs & Others, NKP (2057), No. 6, P. 462, DN: 6013

Case: Relating to void of Unconstitutional law Plaintiff: Meera Dhungana et.al Defendant: Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs & Others Decision Number: 6013

The case is relating to equal property rights of sons and daughters and discrimination against daughters in parental property under the Muluki Ain, 2020.

Facts: Meera Kumari Dhungana and Meera Khanal challenged Section 16 of the Partition Chapter of the Muluki Ain, 2020, which governed the property rights of daughters. Under the provision, an unmarried daughter could receive a share of her parental property only after reaching the age of 35 years and subject to conditions relating to her marital status. The law also contained provisions concerning the return of property if the daughter subsequently married. The position of a son was different. A son could generally claim a share in his father's property without having to wait until a particular age or satisfy the same conditions imposed on a daughter. The petitioners also challenged the use of the word “son” in other provisions of the Partition Chapter. These provisions gave sons a direct position in the inheritance system while daughters were required to satisfy additional conditions before obtaining parental property. At the time, these provisions operated as part of a wider family-property and inheritance system in which property rights were connected with marriage, family relationships and the traditional structure of the household. The petitioners challenged these provisions under the constitutional guarantee of equality in Article 11 of the Constitution of the Kingdom of Nepal, 1990. They also relied on CEDAW, which recognises equality between men and women in property and civil matters. Plaintiff's Claims: The petitioners claimed that the law discriminated against daughters because a son could obtain a share in parental property without an age restriction, while an unmarried daughter had to wait until 35 and satisfy additional conditions. They argued that the discriminatory provisions should be declared invalid and that daughters should have property rights equal to those of sons. Defendants' Arguments: The Government argued that the law did not completely deny daughters property rights. An unmarried daughter could receive property after meeting the legal conditions, while a married daughter could obtain property through her husband's family. The Government also argued that giving a married daughter the same immediate right as a son could allow her to receive property from both her parental and husband's families and create another form of inequality. It further argued that the property system was interconnected and should not be changed by removing one provision without considering the wider legal and social system. Legal Questions:
  1. Whether Section 16 of the Partition Chapter violated the constitutional right to equality.
  2. Whether requiring an unmarried daughter to reach 35 before receiving parental property was discriminatory.
  3. Whether the provisions giving sons a different position in inheritance were unconstitutional.
  4. Whether the Court could direct the Government to reform the wider property and inheritance system.
Different Court Decisions: Supreme Court: The Special Bench did not declare Section 16 invalid. The Court held that the provision did not completely deprive daughters of property rights but regulated those rights differently according to their marital status within the existing family-property system. The Court considered that a married daughter could obtain property through her husband's family, while an unmarried daughter could claim property from her father after satisfying the conditions prescribed by law. It also considered the Government's concern that giving a married daughter an immediate right to parental property in the same manner as a son could allow her to claim property from both families. However, the Court recognised the need for a broader examination of the property and inheritance laws. Rather than striking down one provision in isolation, it directed the Government to study the issue more comprehensively. The Government was directed to consult women's organisations, sociologists, social organisations and lawyers, examine relevant laws of other countries, and prepare a suitable bill for broader legal reform within one year. The petition to invalidate Section 16 was therefore not granted, but a directive for wider legal reform was issued. Principles Established:
  1. Equality does not always require identical treatment in every situation.
  2. Property and inheritance laws should be examined as a connected legal system.
  3. Removing one provision without considering related laws may create further legal inequality.
  4. Laws affecting property rights should be reviewed when they create unequal treatment between men and women.
  5. Constitutional equality should guide the reform of discriminatory laws.
  6. Courts may direct the Government to undertake broader legislative reform.
  7. Traditional family structures cannot by themselves provide a permanent justification for unequal legal rights.

title: Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sunil Babu Panta vs. Government of Nepal & Others, NKP (7th Semester)
content:
Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sunil Babu Panta vs. Government of Nepal & Others, NKP (2064), No.4, DN: 7958

Case: Certiorari, Mandamus and others Plaintiff: Sunil Babu Panta Defendant: Government of Nepal & Others Decision Number: 7958

The case is relating to the constitutional rights of LGBTQI people, including equality, gender identity, privacy, dignity, and protection from discrimination.

  Facts: Sunil Babu Pant, the Executive Director of Blue Diamond Society, filed a public-interest writ petition against the Government of Nepal. The petition was filed on behalf of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex people and others with different sexual orientations and gender identities. At the time, many people in these communities faced discrimination and social exclusion. Some also faced violence, harassment and humiliation. These problems existed within families, society and public institutions. They also faced difficulties in obtaining citizenship, passports and voter documents. Access to education, employment and public services was also difficult for some people. People whose gender identity did not fit into the traditional male or female categories faced additional problems. Officials often had no clear system for recording their gender identity. As a result, some people received official documents that did not match their identity. The petition also raised concerns about the treatment of same-sex relationships. The existing legal and social system largely recognised heterosexual relationships. Same-sex relationships between consenting adults did not receive the same legal recognition and protection. The petitioners relied on the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Interim Constitution of Nepal, 2007. These included the rights to equality, dignity, liberty and privacy. They also relied on international human-rights instruments binding on Nepal, including the ICCPR and ICESCR. Plaintiff's Claims: The petitioners claimed that people with different sexual orientations and gender identities were entitled to the same constitutional rights as everyone else. They argued that discrimination and denial of identity documents violated their rights to equality, dignity, privacy and liberty. They asked the Court to recognise a third-gender category. They also sought identity documents based on a person's gender identity. They asked for protection from discrimination and violence. They further requested a committee to study the legal recognition of same-sex marriage. Defendants' Arguments: The Government and Parliament argued that constitutional rights were already available to all citizens. They said that the petitioners could obtain citizenship and other documents under the existing law. They also argued that the petition did not clearly identify a specific discriminatory law or government action. They maintained that creating or changing laws was mainly the responsibility of Parliament. They therefore asked the Court to dismiss the petition. Legal Questions:
  1. Whether LGBTI people are entitled to the same constitutional rights as other citizens.
  2. Whether denying or restricting identity documents based on gender identity violates equality and identity rights.
  3. Whether consensual sexual relationships between adults are protected by privacy and personal liberty.
  4. Whether the State has a duty to create or amend laws to protect LGBTI people from discrimination.
  Different Court Decisions: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court held that the petition was a genuine public-interest case. It concerned a socially marginalised group whose members faced difficulties in protecting their rights individually. The Court recognised that people with different sexual orientations and gender identities are entitled to the same fundamental rights as other citizens. It held that the State could not discriminate against a person because of their sexual orientation or gender identity. The Court also recognised the right to privacy in consensual relationships between adults. It held that such relationships fall within personal freedom. The State could not interfere merely because the relationship was between people of the same sex. The Court also addressed gender identity. It directed the State to make appropriate arrangements for people whose gender identity did not fit into the traditional male or female categories. The Government was directed to make or amend laws and administrative arrangements so that LGBTI people could enjoy their rights without discrimination. The Court also directed the Government to form a committee to study the legal and social aspects of same-sex marriage. The committee was to make recommendations on its possible legal recognition. The petition was allowed in important respects. The Court issued directive orders for the protection of LGBTI rights and necessary legal reform. Principles Established:
  1. LGBTI people are entitled to the same fundamental rights as other citizens.
  2. Sexual orientation and gender identity cannot be grounds for unconstitutional discrimination.
  3. A person's gender identity must be respected.
  4. People have a right to identity and appropriate official documents.
  5. Privacy protects consensual intimate relationships between adults.
  6. Personal liberty includes the freedom to choose intimate relationships.
  7. Social prejudice, tradition or culture cannot justify denying fundamental rights.
  8. The State must create appropriate legal and administrative arrangements for equal enjoyment of rights.
  9. Public-interest litigation can protect the rights of socially marginalised groups.

title: Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Jyoti Paudel vs. Government of Nepal & Others, NKP (7th Semester)
content:
Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Jyoti Paudel vs. Government of Nepal & Others, NKP (2065), No. 4, P. 485, DN: 8282. Case: Mandamus Plaintiff: Jyoti Paudel Defendant: Government of Nepal & Others Decision Number: 8282

This case is relating to domestic violence, acid attacks against women, protection of women’s rights, and the State’s obligations under CEDAW.

Facts of the Case: The Women Rehabilitation Centre and Advocate Jyoti Paudel filed the petition concerning violence against women, including acid attacks suffered by Sadina Khatun and Rita Devi Mahato. Sadina Khatun was beaten by her husband while breastfeeding her three-year-old daughter. He then threw acid at her, which also affected the child. Sadina suffered severe burns and permanent disfigurement to her face and hands. She approached the police, but no effective action was taken. Rita Devi Mahato was also attacked with acid. She suffered severe burns to her face, neck, and arms. She lost the sight of one eye and was left with permanent injuries and disfigurement. The attack also caused social humiliation and difficulties in her daily life. The petitioners argued that such violence was linked to social attitudes that treated wives and daughters-in-law as inferior to men. The existing law did not adequately address serious domestic violence such as acid attacks or provide proper investigation, prosecution, punishment, treatment, compensation, and rehabilitation. Plaintiff’s Claims: The petitioners claimed that the State had failed to adequately protect women from domestic violence and discrimination. They argued that Nepal had also failed to properly fulfil its obligations under CEDAW. They asked the Court to order effective laws and systems for investigation, prosecution, punishment, treatment, compensation, rehabilitation, legal assistance, and protection of women victims. Defendants’ Arguments: The Home Ministry argued that existing laws applied equally to everyone and that no specific violation of rights had been shown. The Prime Minister’s Office said that the Government was already working to control violence against women and that law-making was mainly the legislature’s responsibility. The Ministry of Law argued that acid attacks were already punishable under existing laws. The Ministry of Women, Children and Social Welfare stated that a draft domestic-violence law was being considered. Legal Questions:
  1. Whether the existing law adequately protected women from domestic violence and acid attacks.
  2. Whether Nepal had fulfilled its obligations under CEDAW.
  3. Whether the existing punishment and legal procedures were sufficient for serious domestic violence.
  4. Whether the State should provide victims with effective remedies, including treatment, compensation, legal assistance, rehabilitation, and speedy justice.
  Different Court Decisions: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court held that the case involved both public interest and the personal rights of the two injured women. It found that the existing legal system did not adequately protect women from serious domestic violence and acid attacks. The Court noted that the Domestic Violence Act did not clearly cover acid attacks within its definition of domestic violence. It also lacked clear procedures for investigation, prosecution, and evidence collection. The punishment was inadequate for serious forms of violence and did not provide an effective deterrent or sufficient justice to victims. The Court held that Nepal could not ignore its obligations under CEDAW after ratifying the Convention. Under the Nepal Treaty Act, international treaty obligations could prevail where applicable domestic law conflicted with them. Therefore, the State had a duty to establish effective laws and mechanisms to protect women. The Court issued directive orders to the Government to broaden the definition of domestic violence, provide effective punishment, and establish clear procedures for investigation and prosecution. It also directed the State to provide free legal assistance to women victims and recommended the use of trained women police officers in investigating such cases. The Court further directed the Government to consider a separate fast-track court for cases involving violence against women. A four-member committee was formed to study the necessary laws, staff, budget, and infrastructure and submit its recommendations. The Court did not determine the criminal guilt of the persons responsible for the acid attacks or impose criminal punishment on them. Principles Established:
  1. Domestic violence is a human-rights violation, not merely a private family matter.
  2. Nepal must implement its international treaty obligations, including CEDAW, in good faith.
  3. Women must not be treated as inferior because they are wives or daughters-in-law.
  4. Acid attacks are serious forms of violence requiring effective legal protection.
  5. Laws must provide effective investigation, prosecution, punishment, and remedies.
  6. Punishment for serious violence should have a real deterrent effect.
  7. Victims of violence should have access to treatment, compensation, legal assistance, protection, and rehabilitation.
  8. The State must take steps to address social practices that discriminate against women.
  9. Special procedures, including fast-track courts, may be used to provide speedy and dignified justice to women victims.
  10. Courts may issue directive orders where existing laws and mechanisms fail to adequately protect fundamental rights and treaty obligations.

title: Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sapana Pradhan Malla vs. Office of Prime Minister & Others, ΝΚΡ (7th Semester)
content:
Gender and Inclusive Justice Case: Sapana Pradhan Malla vs. Office of Prime Minister & Others, ΝΚΡ (2064) No. 9, P. 1208, DN: 7880

Case: Mandamus and others Plaintiff: Sapana Pradhan Malla Defendant: Office of Prime Minister & Others Decision Number: 7880

This case is relating to the right to privacy, confidentiality in legal proceedings, protection of vulnerable victims, and the balance between privacy and fair trial rights.

Facts of the Case: Sapana Pradhan Malla filed a public-interest writ petition on behalf of the Forum for Women, Law and Development. The petition concerned privacy protection for women, children, and people living with HIV/AIDS involved in legal proceedings. Although the Constitution recognised the right to privacy, there was no detailed system to protect the names, identities, addresses, health information, family details, and other personal information of vulnerable persons involved in cases. Women involved in sexual or domestic violence cases could face social stigma, discrimination, threats, and further harm if their identities were disclosed. Children could face long-term stigma from the disclosure of personal or family information. People living with HIV/AIDS could also face discrimination affecting their employment, property, family relationships, and access to treatment. Existing law allowed some cases to be heard in camera. However, the petitioners argued that this did not protect privacy during investigation, registration of cases, inspection of records, copying of documents, media reporting, judgment publication, and enforcement. Plaintiff’s Claims: The petitioners claimed that privacy was closely connected with dignity, equality, liberty, and access to justice. They argued that people may avoid reporting crimes or seeking legal remedies if their personal information is exposed. They asked the Court to order a comprehensive system protecting confidentiality throughout the legal process, along with remedies for unlawful disclosure. Defendants’ Arguments: The Government argued that the petitioners had not shown a specific violation of their own rights and that law-making was mainly Parliament’s responsibility. The Ministry of Law argued that privacy was already protected by the Constitution and that existing court rules allowed some cases to be heard in camera. It also argued that a person whose privacy was violated could seek a legal remedy. Legal Questions:
  1. Whether the right to privacy includes protection of personal identity and confidential information.
  2. Whether women, children, and people living with HIV/AIDS require special privacy protection in legal proceedings.
  3. Whether an in-camera hearing alone is sufficient to protect privacy.
  4. Whether the Government should establish detailed laws and procedures to protect confidentiality throughout legal proceedings.
Different Court Decisions: Supreme Court: The Supreme Court held that the right to privacy protects not only physical privacy but also personal identity, health information, family details, character, address, and other confidential information. The Court recognised that disclosure of such information could expose women, children, and people living with HIV/AIDS to stigma, discrimination, violence, and other harm. Such risks could also discourage victims from reporting crimes or seeking legal remedies. The Court held that an in-camera hearing means more than simply preventing the public from entering the courtroom. Judges, court staff, lawyers, police, prosecutors, and others involved in the case must also maintain confidentiality. Privacy protection may be necessary throughout the legal process, including investigation, hearing, judgment, publication, and enforcement. The Court also held that privacy must be balanced with the accused’s right to a fair trial. Protecting a victim’s identity does not remove the accused’s right to know and challenge the evidence necessary for their defence. The Court directed the Government to form a committee with representatives from relevant institutions and civil society to study the issue and help prepare detailed legislation. Until such legislation was made, the Court directed the Government and relevant courts to follow interim guidelines for protecting privacy and confidentiality. Principles Established:
  1. The right to privacy includes protection of personal identity and confidential information.
  2. Privacy covers information relating to health, family, address, character, custody, and other personal matters.
  3. Vulnerable groups may require special privacy protection against stigma and discrimination.
  4. Privacy is closely connected with dignity, equality, liberty, and access to justice.
  5. An in-camera hearing involves confidentiality beyond simply closing the courtroom to the public.
  6. Privacy protection should begin from investigation and case registration, not only during trial.
  7. Confidentiality may need to continue through judgment publication and enforcement.
  8. The right to information and freedom of expression do not automatically override privacy rights.
  9. Privacy must be balanced with the accused’s right to a fair trial.
  10. Courts can take measures to protect the identity and privacy of victims and parties when necessary.
  11. The Government has a duty to establish effective laws and procedures for protecting privacy.
  12. Courts may issue interim guidelines where detailed legislation is not yet available.
